docs.title: 安全与保护（Security and Protection）
docs.text:
Overview

本讲涵盖可信计算基础、攻击面、访问控制、认证授权以及常见安全攻击等内容。

docs.title: 可信计算基（Trusted Computing Base, TCB）
docs.text:
TCB 问题

  • TCB 越大，越难确保安全
  • TCB 应该尽可能简单： 1. 最小化误用 2. 实现更好的验证

docs.title: 攻击面（Attack Surface）
docs.text:
定义

攻击面是未授权用户可以访问系统并提取数据的所有可能点或攻击向量的数量。

原则

攻击面越小，越容易保护。

docs.title: 认证（Authentication）
docs.text:
目的

识别用户身份。

docs.title: 授权（Authorization）
docs.text:
目的

确定用户和程序对资源的访问权限。

docs.title: 访问控制矩阵
docs.text:
| Object | User1 | User2 | User3 |
|--------|-------|-------|-------|
| File1  |  R,W  |  R    |       |
| File2  |  R    |  R,W  |  R    |
| File3  |  R,W  |  R,W  |  R,W  |
...

问题

矩阵太大，无法存储在内存中。

docs.title: 基于角色的访问控制（RBAC）
docs.text:
原理

每个用户分配到一个角色，每个角色分配一组权限。

docs.title: POSIX 文件权限
docs.text:
用户可以分配到三种类型的角色：

角色 描述 文件拥有者 Owner 文件拥有组 Group 其他用户组 Others

权限位

每个文件只需要用 9 个 bit：3 种权限（读-写-执行）× 3 类用户

docs.title: 何时检查用户权限？
docs.text:
每次打开文件时，进行权限检查和授权：

  1. open() 包含可读/可写的参数，OS 根据用户组进行检查
  2. 引入 fd，记录本次打开权限（授权），作为后续操作的参数

每次操作文件时，根据 fd 信息进行检查。

docs.title: setuid
docs.text:
Linux 密码存储

  • passwd 在 /etc/shadow
  • 只有 root 可以读/写
  • passwd 是 setuid root
  • passwd 可以读/写 /etc/shadow

如何确保 passwd 在被赋予 root 权限时不被恶意用户修改？

  1. SUID：在 passwd 的 inode 中增加一个 SUID 位，使得用户仅在执行该程序时才会被提权，执行完后恢复，从而将进程提权的时间降至最小 - su - passwd
  2. passwd 程序本身的逻辑会保证某一个用户只能修改其自身的密码

docs.title: 能力（Capabilities）
docs.text:
细粒度权限控制

提供细粒度控制进程的权限：基本思想是把 root 的能力拆分，分为几十个小的能力，称为 capability。

缺点

  • 理想状态：41 个 capabilities 均分 root 能力
  • 现实：CAP_SYS_ADMIN 占据了 ⅓ 的 permission checks
  • New Root
  • 使用混乱

docs.title: 审计（Auditing）
docs.text:
目的

记录用户和程序正在做什么，以便后续分析。

docs.title: 引用监视器（Reference Monitor）
docs.text:
关键要求

  • 引用监视器机制必须保证其不可被绕过（Non-bypassable）
  • 设计者必须充分考虑应用访问对象的所有可能路径，并保证所有路径都必须通过引用才能进行

文件系统示例

应用必须通过文件描述符来访问文件，而无法直接访问磁盘上的数据或通过 inode 号来访问文件数据。文件系统此时就是引用监视器，文件描述符就是引用。

docs.title: 代码注入攻击（Code Injection Attack）
docs.text:
攻击方式

图中 buffer 在栈分配，攻击者 overflow — 通过禁止栈的 x 权限来防护。

绕过方法

可以通过先攻击页表来解决。

docs.title: 代码重用攻击（Code Reuse Attack）
ROP 攻击
docs.text:
定义

ROP（Return-Oriented Programming）攻击是一种代码重用攻击。它操纵栈来执行程序中已存在的代码。

docs.title: JOP 攻击
docs.text:
定义

JOP（Jump-Oriented Programming）攻击是一种代码重用攻击。它操纵栈来执行程序中已存在的代码。

防护措施

  • 保护返回地址
  • 保护函数指针

docs.title: 非控制数据攻击（Non-control-data Attack）
docs.text:
int ss_initialized;
{
    ...
    if (!ss_initialized) {
        goto allow;
    }
    ...
}

攻击方式

通过修改 ss_initialized = 0 直接 goto。

docs.title: OS Structure
docs.text:
Overview

This lecture covers the system call interface, ELF file format, linking/loading, and OS structure designs.

docs.title: System Calls
docs.text:
Definition

A system call is an interface provided by the kernel to user space for privileged operations.

docs.title: System Call Number
docs.text:
Key Concepts

Concept Description Syscall Number Unique ID for each syscall Syscall Table Array of function pointers indexed by number OS-Specific Numbers differ across operating systems

docs.title: Example: write() System Call
docs.text:
Execution Flow

  1. User calls printf() → internally calls write()
  2. write() triggers syscall with number 0x1
  3. Enter kernel space:
    • kernel_entry saves all user registers
    • Look up handler in syscall_table
    • Execute handler
  4. ret_to_user:
    • Restore user registers
    • Return to user space
SYSCALL_DEFINE3(write, unsigned int, fd, const char __user *, buf, size_t, count)
{
    return ksys_write(fd, buf, count);
}

docs.title: System Call Implementation
docs.text:
System-call Interface

  • Maintains a table indexed by syscall numbers
  • Each entry points to the syscall handler
  • Caller doesn't need to know implementation details

docs.title: Example: Copying a File
docs.text:
Useful Commands

# Trace system calls
strace cp file1 file2

# Count syscalls
strace -c cp file1 file2

# Count lines of syscall output
strace cp main.c main.copy 2>&1 | wc -l  # ~175 lines
  • 2>&1 — Redirect stderr to stdout
  • | wc -l — Count lines

docs.title: Parameter Passing Methods
docs.text:
Three Methods

Method Description Used By Registers Pass in CPU registers Simple, limited params Block/Table Store in memory, pass address Linux, Solaris Stack Push onto stack No param limit

docs.title: Linkers and Loaders
docs.text:
Distinction

  • Linker: Static linking (compile time)
  • Loader: Dynamic linking (runtime)

docs.title: ELF File Sections
docs.text:
Section Contents .text Executable code .data Initialized global variables .rodata Read-only data (constants) .bss Uninitialized variables

Why .bss instead of .data?

.bss saves space—it's not stored in the ELF file, only initialized to 0 at runtime.

docs.title: Reading ELF Headers
docs.text:
readelf -h main

Key Fields

  • Entry Address: Where execution starts
  • Magic Number: 0x7f 0x45 0x4c 0x46 = "ELF"

docs.title: Static Linking
docs.text:
Characteristics

  • All code packed into single binary
  • Large file size
  • Highly portable

docs.title: Dynamic Linking
docs.text:
Characteristics

  • Reuses shared libraries
  • Smaller ELF size
  • Requires library at runtime
# View dynamic linker path
readelf -p .interp main

Dynamic Linker

The loader (ld-linux-aarch64.so.1) resolves library calls like printf().

docs.title: Memory Regions
docs.text:
Region Permissions Description .text r-xp Readable, executable .rodata r--p Readable only .data rw-p Readable, writable .bss rw-p Initialized to 0 at runtime stack/heap rw-p Anonymous mapping

Memory Layout

  • These mappings are in user space
  • Kernel space has its own: kernel code, kernel data, kernel stack

docs.title: Setup Responsibilities
docs.text:
Who sets up what?

Component Set up by ELF file mapping Kernel (execve()) Stack and heap Kernel (execve()) Libraries Loader

Dynamic linking requires more syscalls than static!

docs.title: Static Binary
docs.text:
objdump -d a.out
  • Entry at 0x400640 is the _start function
  • regs->pc = elf_entry

docs.title: Dynamic Binary
docs.text:
• Entry point is the loader (ld.so), not _start
  • Loader resolves libraries, then jumps to _start

docs.title: OS Portability
docs.text:
Why Apps are OS-Specific

System calls differ across OSes (names, numbers, behavior)

docs.title: Cross-Platform Solutions
docs.text:
Approach Example Interpreted language Python, Ruby Virtual Machine Java Recompilation C code for each OS

ABI vs API

Application Binary Interface (ABI) = architecture-level equivalent of API

Defines how binary components interface for a given OS/architecture.

docs.title: OS Structure Designs
docs.text:
Common Structures

Structure Example Description Simple MS-DOS Minimal layering Monolithic Unix, Linux Everything in kernel Layered — Abstraction layers Microkernel Mach Minimal kernel, services in user space

Helpful Resource

Linux Kernel Map

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
Overview

This lecture covers the process concept, process states, creation/termination, and context switching.

docs.title: Process Concept
docs.text:
Definition

A process is a unit of resource allocation and protection.

docs.title: Process Components
docs.text:
Process = code (text section)
            initially stored on disk in executable file
        + data section
            global variables (.bss and .data)
        + program counter
            points to next instruction
        + processor registers
        + stack
        + heap

┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Stack                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│                ↓                    │
│               ...                   │
│                ↑                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│              Heap                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│              Data                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│              Code                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Stack vs Heap
docs.text:
Pointers

Pointer Points to Stack Pointer (SP) Top of the stack Frame Pointer (FP) Current function's stack frame

Why is stack faster than heap?

Stack contents are often in CPU cache due to locality.

docs.title: Runtime Stack
docs.text: • Two processes can share the same code but have different stacks/heaps

docs.title: Process Control Block (PCB)
docs.text:
Key Facts

  • Each process has exactly one PCB
  • PCB allocated on process creation
  • PCB freed on process termination
  • In Linux: struct task_struct

docs.title: Special Processes
docs.text:
Process 0 and 1

Process Name Description 0 Idle Runs when no other process is running 1 Init (systemd) Parent of all other processes
  • When systemd terminates → system reboots

docs.title: The fork() System Call
docs.text:
Key Behavior

  • Creates a copy of the parent process
  • Child has different pid (and ppid)
  • Resource utilization reset to 0
  • Returns twice: child's pid to parent, 0 to child
pid = fork();
if (pid < 0) {
    fprintf(stderr, "Error: can't fork()\n");
    perror("fork()");
}
if (pid != 0) {
    // PARENT
    fprintf(stdout, "I am parent, child pid: %d\n", pid);
} else {
    // CHILD
    fprintf(stdout, "I am child, my pid: %d\n", getpid());
}

Memory Isolation Example

int a = 12;
if (pid = fork()) {  // PARENT
    sleep(10);
    printf("a = %d\n", a);  // Prints 12!
} else {  // CHILD
    a += 3;
    while(1);
}

Parent prints a = 12 because child cannot modify parent's memory.

docs.title: Fork Quiz
docs.text:
How many times does this print 'Hello'?

pid1 = fork();
printf("Hello\n");
pid2 = fork();
printf("Hello\n");
Answer: 6 times

docs.title: UNIX Process Creation Pattern
docs.text:
Common Pattern

Syscall Purpose fork() Create new process execve() Replace memory with new program wait() Parent waits for child

execve() Behavior

After exec*():

  • Old code, data, stack replaced
  • PID unchanged
  • Code after exec() never runs (if successful)

docs.title: Fork Pros and Cons
docs.text:
Advantages

  • Simple: Windows' CreateProcess needs 10 parameters!
  • Division: fork creates skeleton, exec gives soul
  • Connection: Maintains parent-child relationship

Disadvantages

  • Complex: Two syscalls needed
  • Performance: Overhead of copying
  • Security: Potential issues

docs.title: Wait and Waitpid
docs.text:
Waiting for Children

Function Behavior wait() Blocks until any child completes waitpid() Blocks until specific child completes

Use WNOHANG for non-blocking waitpid().

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
Common Signals

Ctrl+C sends SIGINT

docs.title: Zombie Process
docs.text:
Definition

A zombie is a process that has terminated but whose parent hasn't called wait().

What resources can't a child deallocate?

The PCB — must be deallocated by parent!

Solution: Call wait() or waitpid() in parent.

docs.title: Orphan Process
docs.text:
Definition

An orphan is a process whose parent has terminated.

Orphans are adopted by init (PID 1).

Avoiding Zombies with Double Fork 
if (pid != 0) {
    // Parent - doesn't wait
    while(1);
} else {  // Child
    pid = fork();
    if (pid == 0) {
        // Grandchild
        sleep(10);
        exit(0);  // Becomes orphan, not zombie
    } else {
        sleep(1);
        exit(0);  // Child exits, grandchild orphaned
    }
}

docs.title: Ready Queue and Wait Queues
docs.text:
Queue Types

Queue Contents Ready Queue Processes ready to run (always has idle process) Wait Queue Processes waiting for an event

Implementation

Processes linked via doubly-linked lists. Use offset to find task_struct.

docs.title: Context Switch
docs.text:
Context Switch = Pure Overhead

Should be minimized!

What is Context?

CPU has one register set. Context = saved register values.

docs.title: Context Switch Code
docs.text:
Steps:

  1. Save current process's context to cpu_context in task_struct
  2. x8 points to new process's task_struct
  3. Load new process's context from its cpu_context

When is switch_to() return value set?

Each process has its own saved PC value!

Key Points

  • task_struct is on the heap
  • Context switch happens in kernel mode
  • fork() returns twice because it creates two contexts!

Reference

HobbitQia's Notes on Context Switch

docs.title: Lab Note
docs.text:
Lab Implementation

In lab: do_timer trap → kernel space → schedule() → switch_to() → next process

docs.title: CPU Scheduling
docs.text:
Overview

This lecture covers scheduling algorithms, from simple FCFS to sophisticated multi-level feedback queues, and real-world implementations in Windows and Linux.

docs.title: Preemptive vs Non-preemptive
docs.text:
Definitions

Type Description Non-preemptive Process runs until completion or self-blocking Preemptive OS can interrupt and move process to ready queue

docs.title: Preemptive Scheduling
docs.text:
Advantages

  • No need for processes to voluntarily yield CPU
  • OS remains in control

Challenges

  • Shared data access synchronization
  • Kernel mode preemption issues
  • Interrupt handling during critical operations

docs.title: Scheduling Objectives
docs.text:
Key Metrics

Metric Goal Definition CPU Utilization Maximize Fraction of time CPU is busy Throughput Maximize Work completed per time unit Turnaround Time Minimize Creation → Completion Waiting Time Minimize Time in READY state Response Time Minimize Creation → First response

docs.title: Dispatcher
docs.text:
Dispatcher Module

Gives CPU control to the process selected by scheduler:

  1. Switch to kernel mode
  2. Context switch
  3. Switch to user mode
  4. Jump to user program location

Dispatch Latency

Time to stop one process and start another.

docs.title: Gantt Chart
docs.text:
Visualization Tool

Timeline showing when each process runs—useful for analyzing algorithm performance.

docs.title: First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)
docs.text:
Characteristics

  • Simplest algorithm
  • Non-preemptive
  • Processes scheduled in arrival order

Convoy Effect

Short processes get stuck behind long processes!

docs.title: Shortest-Job-First (SJF)
docs.text:
Principle

Schedule process with shortest next CPU burst.

docs.title: Preemptive SJF (SRTF)
docs.text:
Optimality

SJF is provably optimal for average wait time!

Big Problem

How do we know burst durations?

Solution: Exponential averaging of past bursts.

docs.title: Round Robin (RR)
docs.text:
Mechanism

  • Each process gets a time quantum
  • If not complete → move to end of ready queue
  • Ready queue is FIFO

Time Quantum Trade-off

Quantum Effect Too large Degenerates to FCFS Too small Context switch overhead dominates

Practical Values

  • Time quantum: 10-100 ms
  • Context switch: ~10 μs
  • CPU time on switching: very low

docs.title: Priority Scheduling
docs.text:
Mechanism

  • Each process assigned a priority
  • Highest priority runs first
  • Can combine with Round Robin for equal priorities

Problem: Starvation

Low-priority processes may never execute!

Solution: Aging

Increase priority as time passes.

docs.title: Multilevel Queue Scheduling
docs.text:
Structure

One ready queue per class of processes.

Scheduling within queues:

  • Each queue has its own policy (e.g., RR for high-priority, FCFS for low)

Scheduling between queues:

  • Preemptive priority (process runs only if higher queues empty)
  • Or time-slicing (e.g., 80% to Q1, 20% to Q2)

docs.title: Multilevel Feedback Queue
docs.text:
Example: Three Queues

Queue Quantum Type Q0 8 RR (highest priority) Q1 16 RR Q2 FCFS (lowest priority)

Process flow:

  1. New process → Q0 (quantum = 8)
  2. Doesn't use all quantum → Likely I/O-bound, stay in Q0
  3. Uses all quantum → Demote to Q1 (quantum = 16)
  4. Uses all → Demote to Q2 (CPU-bound, runs when others don't need CPU)

docs.title: Multiple-Processor Scheduling
docs.text:
Processor Affinity

Type Description Soft affinity OS attempts to keep thread on same processor Hard affinity Process specifies allowed processor set

docs.title: Windows Scheduling
docs.text:
Windows Characteristics

  1. Priority-based, time-quantum, multi-queue, preemptive
  2. 32-level priority (higher number = higher priority)
  3. Waking threads get priority boost (likely I/O-bound)
  4. Idle thread: "Bogus" thread that runs when nothing else can
    • Simplifies OS design (no "no process running" case)

docs.title: Linux Scheduling
docs.text:
Linux Characteristics

  • Lower number = higher priority (opposite of Windows!)

Linux 0.11 Drawbacks

  1. \(O(n)\) scheduling algorithm
  2. Responsiveness not guaranteed

Details

See lecture slides [05 scheduling.pdf]

docs.title: 进程间通信（Inter-Process Communication）
docs.text:
概述

本讲介绍进程间通信（IPC）的主要机制，包括消息传递、共享内存、信号、管道和客户端-服务器通信。

docs.title: 消息传递（Message Passing）
docs.text:
性能开销

消息传递的开销较高：每次通信操作都需要一次系统调用。

为什么需要系统调用？因为需要从用户态切换到内核态来访问内核的数据结构。

需要实现两个基本操作：

操作 描述 send(Q, message) 向进程 Q 发送消息 recv(Q, message) 从进程 Q 接收消息

docs.title: 直接通信（Direct Communication）
docs.text:
特点

进程必须显式命名对方：

  • send(P, message) – 向进程 P 发送消息
  • receive(Q, message) – 从进程 Q 接收消息
  • 每对进程之间恰好存在一条链接

缺点

需要建立大量链接，扩展性差。

docs.title: 间接通信（Indirect Communication）
docs.text:
邮箱机制

消息通过邮箱（mailbox）或端口（port） 进行收发：

  • 每个邮箱有唯一标识符
  • 进程只有共享同一邮箱时才能通信
特性 描述 链接建立 仅当进程共享公共邮箱时建立 关联性 一条链接可关联多个进程 多链接 每对进程可共享多条通信链接 方向性 链接可以是单向或双向的

docs.title: 同步（Synchronization）
docs.text:
同步方式

消息传递可以是阻塞（同步） 或非阻塞（异步） 的。

docs.title: 缓冲（Buffering）
docs.text:
消息队列附加在链接上，有三种实现方式：

容量类型 描述 发送者行为 零容量 链接上不排队任何消息 必须等待接收者 有界容量 有限长度，最多 n 条消息 链接满时必须等待 无界容量 无限长度 永不等待

docs.title: 共享内存（Shared Memory）
docs.text:
工作原理

  1. 一个进程创建共享内存段
  2. 其他进程将其"附加"到自己的地址空间
  3. 进程通过读写共享内存区域进行通信

安全注意

这实际上与多道程序设计的核心思想——内存保护相违背！

  • 进程自行负责协调，不互相干扰
  • 操作系统完全不参与

docs.title: 相关系统调用
docs.text:
shmget()   // 创建/获取共享内存段
shmat()    // 附加共享内存到进程地址空间
shmdt()    // 分离共享内存
shmctl()   // 控制共享内存段

缺点

  1. 进程必须自行协调对共享内存的访问
  2. 无法防护其他进程：一旦其他进程获得共享内存段的 ID，就可以附加并读写它

docs.title: 信号（Signals）
docs.text:
回顾

在 Lecture 4 中，我们讨论了一个进程如何被另一个进程终止。信号就是实现这一功能的机制。

docs.title: 普通管道（Ordinary Pipes）
docs.text:
特点

普通管道无法从创建它的进程外部访问。

通常，父进程创建管道，用于与其创建的子进程通信。

docs.title: 命名管道（Named Pipes）
docs.text:
命名管道的优势

命名管道比普通管道更强大：

特性 描述 双向通信 支持双向数据传输 无亲缘关系要求 通信进程之间不需要父子关系 多进程支持 多个进程可使用同一命名管道通信 跨平台 UNIX 和 Windows 系统都提供支持

docs.title: 管道示例：ls | grep foo
docs.text:
Shell 如何执行这条命令？

详细执行流程

步骤 1：fork() 创建第一个子进程

Shell 首先创建一个子进程来执行 ls 命令。

步骤 2：创建管道（pipe）

在 fork() 之后，shell 创建一个管道，管道有两个文件描述符：

  • 写端（供 ls 使用）
  • 读端（供 grep 使用）

步骤 3：子进程 1（ls）

在子进程中：

  • 关闭标准输出（stdout），将其重定向到管道的写端
  • 关闭管道的读端（子进程不需要读）
  • 使用 exec() 替换进程镜像，执行 ls 命令

步骤 4：fork() 创建第二个子进程

Shell 创建第二个子进程来运行 grep foo。

步骤 5：子进程 2（grep）

在第二个子进程中：

  • 关闭标准输入（stdin），将其重定向到管道的读端
  • 关闭管道的写端（子进程不需要写）
  • 使用 exec() 替换进程镜像，执行 grep foo 命令

步骤 6：父进程（Shell）

  • 关闭管道的写端和读端（父进程不直接参与管道的读写）
  • 等待两个子进程结束

步骤 7-10：执行与完成

  • ls 写入管道 → grep 从管道读取 → ls 完成 → grep 完成

docs.title: Thread
docs.text:
Overview

Threads are lightweight execution units within a process, enabling concurrency with shared memory.

docs.title: Thread Concept
docs.text:
Definition

A thread is a basic unit of execution within a process.

线程是进程内的基本执行单元，进程是资源分配和保护的基本单元

Key Point

A process contains at least one thread, and can contain multiple threads.

docs.title: What Threads Share
docs.text:
Shared Resources

Resource Shared? Code section ✓ Data section ✓ Heap ✓ Open files ✓ Signals ✓

docs.title: What Threads DON'T Share
docs.text:
Private to Each Thread

Resource Shared? Registers ✗ Stack ✗ Program Counter ✗ Thread ID ✗

docs.title: Economy
docs.text:
Resource Efficiency

Operation Thread Process Creation Cheap (code/data/heap already loaded) Expensive Context Switch Cheap (no cache flush) Expensive

docs.title: Resource Sharing
docs.text:
Natural Memory Sharing

  • Threads share memory automatically
  • No need for complex IPC mechanisms
  • Much simpler than shared memory segments

docs.title: Responsiveness
docs.text:
Better User Experience

  • One thread can handle user input while another computes
  • Example: Server spawns thread for each client request

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Parallelism

Multi-threaded processes can do multiple things at once.

Having concurrent activities in the same address space is powerful—but fraught with danger!

docs.title: Drawbacks of Threads
docs.text:
Poor Isolation

  • One thread crash can bring down entire process
  • Shared memory means bugs can corrupt other threads' data

docs.title: Threading Models
docs.text:
Linux Model

Linux uses One-to-One model.

docs.title: Many-to-One Model
docs.text:
Limitations

  • If one thread blocks → all threads block
  • Can't utilize multiple CPUs

docs.title: One-to-One Model
docs.text:
Advantages

  • No blocking issues
  • True parallelism on multi-CPU

Disadvantages

  • Creating thread requires kernel work
  • Slower than Many-to-One

Examples

Linux, Windows, Solaris 9+

docs.title: 同步（Synchronization）
docs.text:
Overview

本讲涵盖竞态条件、临界区问题、硬件同步支持以及各种同步原语（互斥锁、信号量等）。

docs.title: 竞态条件（Race Condition）
docs.text:
定义

当多个进程（或线程）并发访问和操作同一数据，且执行结果取决于访问的特定顺序时，称为竞态条件。

单核也会有竞态条件

由于中断的存在！

docs.title: 临界区（Critical Section）
docs.text:
核心规则

只有一个进程可以在临界区中

  • 当一个进程在临界区时，其他进程不能进入它的临界区
  • 每个进程必须在入口区（entry section）请求进入临界区的许可
  • 许可应该在出口区（exit section）释放
  • 剩余区（Remainder section）

docs.title: 单核系统中如何保护临界区？
docs.text:
停止中断？

在单核系统中可以通过禁用中断来实现保护。

多核系统

在多核系统中，临界区保护只能通过同步来实现。

docs.title: 临界区问题的三个要求 [重要！]
docs.text:
1. 互斥（Mutual Exclusion）

只有一个进程可以在临界区中执行。

2. 前进（Progress）

如果没有进程在其临界区中执行，并且有些进程希望进入它们的临界区，那么只有那些不在剩余区执行的进程可以参与决定下一个进入的进程，且这个选择不能无限期推迟。

3. 有界等待（Bounded Waiting）

在一个进程请求进入其临界区之后，在该请求被批准之前，其他进程进入其临界区的次数存在上限。

这防止了饥饿（starvation）。

docs.title: Peterson 算法
docs.text:
限制

  • 只适用于两个进程！
  • 假设 LOAD 和 STORE 是原子操作

两个进程共享两个变量：

  • boolean flag[2]：进程是否准备进入临界区
  • int turn：轮到谁进入临界区

证明

性质 证明 互斥性 前进性 有界等待

注意

不能调整代码顺序，否则可能会出现问题。

docs.title: Test-and-Set
docs.text:
bool test_set(bool *target) {
    bool rv = *target;
    *target = TRUE;
    return rv;
}

bool lock = FALSE;
do {
    while (test_set(&lock)); // 忙等待
    // 临界区
    lock = FALSE;
    // 剩余区
} while (TRUE);

性质分析

性质 是否满足 互斥 ✓ 前进 ✓ 有界等待 ✗

有界等待的解决方案

docs.title: Compare-and-Swap
docs.text:
int compare_and_swap(int *value, int expected, int new_value) {
    int temp = *value;
    if (*value == expected)
        *value = new_value;
    return temp;
}

特点

  • 原子执行
  • 返回传入参数 value 的原始值
  • 仅当 *value == expected 时才设置变量 value 为 new_value
while (true) {
    while (compare_and_swap(&lock, 0, 1) != 0); /* 空操作 */
    /* 临界区 */
    lock = 0;
    /* 剩余区 */
}

docs.title: 实践中的实现
docs.text:
ARM 的 LDXR 和 STXR 机制

  • LDXR (Load Exclusive Register)：从内存地址加载值，并进入 Exclusive Access 状态（由 local monitor 管理）
  • STXR (Store Exclusive Register)：尝试写入 LDXR 加载的地址，仅当 local monitor 保持 Exclusive Access 状态时才成功
返回状态码 含义 0 成功，Exclusive Access 状态未被破坏 1 失败，Exclusive Access 状态被破坏

docs.title: 原子变量（Atomic Variables）
docs.text:
概念

通常，compare-and-swap 等指令作为其他同步工具的构建块。

原子变量提供对基本数据类型（如整数和布尔值）的原子（不可中断）更新。

void increment(atomic_int *v) {
    int temp;
    do {
        temp = *v;
    } while (temp != (compare_and_swap(v, temp, temp + 1)));
}

docs.title: 互斥锁（Mutex Locks）
docs.text:
bool locked = false;

acquire() {
    while (compare_and_swap(&locked, false, true))
        ; // 忙等待
}

release() {
    locked = false;
}

问题

忙等待效率低下 — 这种锁称为自旋锁（spinlock）

docs.title: 改进方案
docs.text:
void init() {
    flag = 0;
}

void lock() {
    while (test_set(&flag, 1) == 1)
        yield(); // 让出 CPU
}

void unlock() {
    flag = 0;
}

docs.title: 信号量（Semaphores）
docs.text:
改进思路

  • 添加一个队列
  • 当锁被锁定时，将进程状态改为 SLEEP，添加到队列，并调用 schedule()

信号量定义

  • 信号量包含 S — 整数变量
  • 只能通过两个不可分割（原子）操作访问：
  • wait() 和 signal()（原名 P() 和 V()，荷兰语）
wait(S) {
    while (S <= 0); // 忙等待
    S--;
}

signal(S) {
    S++;
}
类型 描述 计数信号量 S 可以在无限制范围内变化 二进制信号量 S 只能是 0 或 1

docs.title: 等待队列实现
docs.text:
typedef struct {
    int value;
    struct list_head *waiting_queue;
} semaphore;

两个操作：

  • block — 将调用操作的进程放入适当的等待队列
  • wakeup — 从等待队列中移除一个进程并放入就绪队列
wait(semaphore *S) {
    S->value--;
    if (S->value < 0) {
        add this process to S->list;
        block();
    }
}

signal(semaphore *S) {
    S->value++;
    if (S->value <= 0) {
        remove a proc P from S->list;
        wakeup(P);
    }
}

注意

wait() 和 signal() 操作是原子操作，不会被中断 — 也需要 Mutex Lock

所以 critical section 没有 busy waiting，但是 wait() 和 signal() 有 busy waiting。

docs.title: 互斥锁 vs 信号量
互斥锁或自旋锁
docs.text:
优点 缺点 无阻塞 在循环上浪费 CPU

适用场景

适合短临界区

docs.title: 信号量
docs.text:
考虑因素

临界区短时 — 频繁的上下文切换很耗时

优点 缺点 无循环 上下文切换耗时

适用场景

适合长临界区

Linux 内核

在 Linux 内核中，spinlock 更常见。

饥饿与死锁

饥饿不一定死锁，但是死锁一定饥饿。

docs.title: 互斥锁
docs.text:
#include <pthread.h>
pthread_mutex_t mutex;

/* 创建并初始化互斥锁 */
pthread_mutex_init(&mutex, NULL);

/* 获取互斥锁 */
pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
/* 临界区 */
/* 释放互斥锁 */
pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

docs.text: • 命名信号量 & 无名信号量

docs.title: 同步经典问题（Synchronization Real World Problems）
docs.text:
概述

本讲介绍三个经典的同步问题：有界缓冲区问题、读者-写者问题和哲学家就餐问题。

docs.title: 有界缓冲区问题（Bounded-Buffer Problem）
docs.text:
问题描述

生产者（Producer） 和 消费者（Consumer） 共享 n 个缓冲区：

  • 生产者生成数据，放入缓冲区
  • 消费者从缓冲区取出数据消费

需要保证

  • 生产者不能向已满的缓冲区添加数据
  • 消费者不能从空的缓冲区移除数据

docs.title: 解决方案
docs.text: 信号量 初始值 作用 mutex 1 互斥访问缓冲区 full-slots 0 已满槽位数 empty-slots N 空槽位数

docs.title: 生产者代码
docs.text:
do {
    // produce an item
    ...
    wait(empty-slots);   // 等待空槽
    wait(mutex);         // 进入临界区
    // add the item to the buffer
    ...
    signal(mutex);       // 离开临界区
    signal(full-slots);  // 增加已满槽位
} while (TRUE);

注意：两个 wait 不能交换顺序！

如果先 wait(mutex) 再 wait(empty-slots)，会导致带锁睡眠！

生产者持有 mutex 后阻塞在 empty-slots 上，消费者无法获取 mutex 来释放槽位，造成死锁。

docs.title: 消费者代码
docs.text:
do {
    wait(full-slots);    // 等待已满槽
    wait(mutex);         // 进入临界区
    // remove an item from buffer
    ...
    signal(mutex);       // 离开临界区
    signal(empty-slots); // 增加空槽位
    // consume the item
    ...
} while (TRUE);

docs.title: 读者-写者问题（Readers-Writers Problem）
docs.text:
问题描述

多个并发进程共享一个数据集：

  • 读者（Readers）：只读取数据，不进行更新
  • 写者（Writers）：可以读取和写入数据

访问规则

  • 允许多个读者同时读取（共享访问）
  • 只允许一个写者访问共享数据（独占访问）

docs.title: 读者优先方案
docs.text:
变量/信号量 初始值 作用 mutex 1 保护 readcount write 1 控制写访问 readcount 0 当前读者数量

方案特点

这是读者优先（Reader First） 方案。

docs.title: 写者代码
docs.text:
do {
    wait(write);
    // writing is performed
    ...
    signal(write);
} while (TRUE);

docs.title: 读者代码
docs.text:
do {
    wait(mutex);
    readcount++;
    if (readcount == 1) wait(write);  // 第一个读者，锁住写者
    signal(mutex);

    // reading is performed
    ...

    wait(mutex);
    readcount--;
    if (readcount == 0) signal(write); // 最后一个读者，释放写锁
    signal(mutex);
} while (TRUE);

代码解析

  • if (readcount == 1) wait(write)：第一个读者进入时，将写者屏蔽在外
  • if (readcount == 0) signal(write)：最后一个读者离开时，释放写锁

docs.title: 场景分析
docs.text:
场景 1：读者排队
  1. 读者 A 先到 → 阻塞在 write 等待队列
  2. 读者 B 到达 → 阻塞在 mutex 等待队列
  3. 读者 C 到达 → 阻塞在 mutex 等待队列
  4. 写者释放 write
  5. A、B、C 依次可以读取
场景 2：读者被中断
  • 读者 A 正在读取数据，被中断
  • 此时调度写者？

答案

  1. 写者在 write 的等待队列中，不在就绪队列
  2. 所以写者不会被调度

docs.title: 读者优先
docs.text: 特点 描述 规则 除非写者正在更新数据，否则读者不等待 行为 如果读者持有数据，新读者直接进入读取 问题 写者可能饥饿

docs.title: 写者优先
docs.text: 特点 描述 规则 一旦写者就绪，尽快执行写操作 行为 如果读者持有数据，新读者等待挂起的写者 问题 读者可能饥饿

docs.title: 写者优先方案
docs.text: 变量/信号量 初始值 作用 readcount, writecount 0 计数器 rmutex 1 保护 readcount wmutex 1 保护 writecount readTry 1 阻止新读者进入 resource 1 资源访问控制

docs.title: 读者代码（写者优先）
docs.text:
reader() {
    // ENTRY Section
    readTry.P();                 // 表示读者尝试进入
    rmutex.P();                  // 锁定入口区
    readcount++;                 
    if (readcount == 1)          // 第一个读者
        resource.P();            // 锁定资源
    rmutex.V();                  
    readTry.V();                 // 完成尝试进入

    // CRITICAL Section
    // reading is performed

    // EXIT Section
    rmutex.P();                  
    readcount--;                 
    if (readcount == 0)          // 最后一个读者
        resource.V();            // 释放资源
    rmutex.V();                  
}

docs.title: 写者代码（写者优先）
docs.text:
writer() {
    // ENTRY Section
    wmutex.P();                  // 锁定入口区
    writecount++;                
    if (writecount == 1)         // 第一个写者
        readTry.P();             // 阻止新读者尝试进入
    wmutex.V();                  
    resource.P();                // 获取资源

    // CRITICAL Section
    // writing is performed
    resource.V();                // 释放资源

    // EXIT Section
    wmutex.P();                  
    writecount--;                
    if (writecount == 0)         // 最后一个写者
        readTry.V();             // 允许读者尝试进入
    wmutex.V();                  
}

docs.title: 哲学家就餐问题（Dining-Philosophers Problem）
docs.text:
问题描述

哲学家们的生活就是思考和吃饭：

  • 他们坐在圆桌旁，彼此不交流
  • 偶尔尝试拿起 2 根筷子（一次拿一根）来吃饭
  • 每两个相邻哲学家之间有一根筷子
  • 需要两根筷子才能吃饭，吃完后放下两根

问题本质

哲学家就餐问题代表了多资源同步问题。

docs.title: 解决方案
docs.text:
参考资料

详见课件 [10-29第7-8节]

常见解决策略

  1. 限制哲学家数量：最多允许 n-1 个哲学家同时尝试就餐
  2. 奇偶策略：奇数号哲学家先拿左边筷子，偶数号先拿右边
  3. 同时获取：只有当两根筷子都可用时才拿起

docs.title: 死锁（Deadlocks）
docs.text:
概述

本讲介绍死锁的必要条件、预防、避免、检测和恢复策略。

docs.title: 死锁的必要条件
docs.text:
四个必要条件

死锁发生必须同时满足以下四个条件：

条件 描述 互斥（Mutual Exclusion） 资源一次只能被一个进程使用 持有并等待（Hold and Wait） 进程持有至少一个资源，同时等待获取其他进程持有的资源 非抢占（No Preemption） 资源只能由持有它的进程在完成任务后自愿释放 循环等待（Circular Wait） 存在一组等待进程 {P₀, P₁, …, Pₙ} 形成循环等待链

循环等待链

  • P₀ 等待 P₁ 持有的资源
  • P₁ 等待 P₂ 持有的资源
  • ...
  • Pₙ₋₁ 等待 Pₙ 持有的资源
  • Pₙ 等待 P₀ 持有的资源

重要提示

循环等待不一定导致死锁，但它是死锁的必要条件。

docs.title: 死锁预防（Deadlock Prevention）
docs.text:
基本思想

破坏四个必要条件中的至少一个。

docs.title: 破坏循环等待条件
docs.text:
最常用的方法

  • 给每个资源（如 mutex 锁）分配一个唯一编号
  • 资源必须按顺序获取

错误示例（会导致死锁）：

/* thread one */
void *do_work_one(void *param) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&first_mutex);
    pthread_mutex_lock(&second_mutex);
    /* Do some work */
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&second_mutex);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&first_mutex);
    pthread_exit(0);
}

/* thread two */
void *do_work_two(void *param) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&second_mutex);  // ❌ 顺序相反
    pthread_mutex_lock(&first_mutex);   // ❌ 可能死锁
    /* Do some work */
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&first_mutex);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&second_mutex);
    pthread_exit(0);
}

正确示例（统一顺序）：

/* thread one */
void *do_work_one(void *param) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&first_mutex);
    pthread_mutex_lock(&second_mutex);
    /* Do some work */
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&second_mutex);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&first_mutex);
    pthread_exit(0);
}

/* thread two */
void *do_work_two(void *param) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&first_mutex);   // ✅ 相同顺序
    pthread_mutex_lock(&second_mutex);  // ✅ 避免死锁
    /* Do some work */
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&second_mutex);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&first_mutex);
    pthread_exit(0);
}

锁排序不总是适用

银行转账案例：

  • A 向 B 转账：先锁 A（from），再锁 B（to）
  • B 向 A 转账：先锁 B（from），再锁 A（to）
  • 如果都按 "先锁 from，再锁 to" 的顺序，会导致死锁！

docs.title: Lec 1  \(\lambda\)-Calculus
docs.text: Lambda calculus is a formal system in mathematical logic for expressing computation based on function abstraction and application using variable binding and substitution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
• Variables: \(x, y, z, \ldots\)
  • Abstraction: \(\lambda x.M\) where \(x\) is a variable and \(M\) is a lambda term.
  • Application: if \(M\) and \(N\) are lambda terms, then \((M N)\) is a lambda term.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
• Identity function: \(\lambda x.x\)
  • Constant function: \(\lambda x.y\)
  • \(\lambda x.(\lambda y.y x)\) is a function that takes two arguments and returns the second one. -- Abstraction (Definition)
  • Example: \((\lambda x.(\lambda y.y x)) a b \rightarrow (\lambda y.y a) b \rightarrow b a\)
  • \((\lambda x.x)y\) is a function that takes one argument and returns the argument. -- Application
  • Example: \((\lambda x.x)y \rightarrow y\)
  • \((\lambda x.x) (\lambda y.y x)\) is a function that takes one argument and returns the identity function. -- Application
  • Example: \((\lambda x.x) (\lambda y.y x) \rightarrow \lambda y.y x\)

docs.title: Free and Bound Variables
docs.text:
• A variable \(x\) is free in \(M\) if \(x\) is not bound by any \(\lambda\) in \(M\).
  • A variable \(x\) is bound in \(M\) if \(x\) is bound by some \(\lambda\) in \(M\).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
• In \(\lambda x.x\), \(x\) is bound.
  • In \(\lambda x.y\), \(y\) is free.
  • In \(\lambda x.y x\), \(x\) is bound and \(y\) is free.
  • In \((\lambda y,y)(\lambda x.xy)\), represented as \(MN\) where \(M = (\lambda y.y)\) and \(N = (\lambda x.xy)\), \(x\) is bound in \(N\) and \(y\) is bound in \(M\).
  • In M: \(y\) is bound.
  • In N: \(x\) is bound and \(y\) is free. also \(y\) has nothing to do with the \(y\) in \(M\).
  • In \(\lambda x.(\lambda y.y xz)\), \(x\) is bound by the first \(\lambda\) and \(y\) is bound by the second \(\lambda\) and \(z\) is free.

docs.title: Free Variable
docs.text:
CANNOT CHANGE NAME OF FREE VARIABLE

  • \(FV(x) = \{x\}\)
  • \(FV(\lambda x.t') = FV(t') - \{x\}\)
  • \(FV(t_1 t_2) = FV(t_1) \cup FV(t_2)\)

docs.title: Bound Variable
docs.text: CAN CHANGE NAME OF BOUND VARIABLE * \(BV(x) = \emptyset\) * \(BV(\lambda x.t') = BV(t') \cup \{x\}\) * \(BV(t_1 t_2) = BV(t_1) \cup BV(t_2)\)

docs.title: Example2
docs.text:
• \(BV(\lambda x.y x) = \{x\}\) ; \(FV(\lambda x.y x) = \{y\}\)
  • \(BV(xyz) = \emptyset\) ; \(FV(xyz) = \{x, y, z\}\)
  • \(BV(\lambda x.\lambda y.x) = \{x,y\}\) ; \(FV(\lambda x.\lambda y.x) = \emptyset\)
  • \(BV(\lambda x.\lambda y.y)=\{x,y\}\) ; \(FV(\lambda x.\lambda y.y) = \emptyset\)

docs.title: Closed Term
docs.text:
• A term with no free variables is called a closed term: \(FV(t) = \emptyset\)
  • Term \(t\) 相对于 term \(t'\)封闭 if and only if \(FV(t) \cap BV(t') = \emptyset\)
  • \(t\) 's free variables are not bound by \(t'\)
  • Closed term s is a closed term relative to any term \(t\).

docs.title: Substitution
docs.text:
• \([N/x]M\) implies that all occurrences of \(x\) in \(M\) are replaced by \(N\).
  • In M, there cannot be any bound variable with the same name as the free variable in N.

docs.title: \(\alpha\)-Renaming
docs.text:
• \(\forall x\) and \(\forall term\ t'\) \(\lambda x.t' =_{\alpha} \lambda y.[y/x]t'\).
  • If \(t' =_{\alpha} t''\), then \(\lambda x.t' =_{\alpha} \lambda x.t''\).
  • If \(t_1 =_{\alpha} t_1'\) and \(t_2 =_{\alpha} t_2'\), then \(t_1 t_2 =_{\alpha} t_1' t_2'\).

docs.title: \(\beta\)-Reduction
docs.text:
• \(\forall x\) and \(\forall term\ t_1'\) and \(t_2\), if \(t_2\) is closed relative to \(t_1'\), then \((\lambda x.t_1')t_2 =_{\beta} [t_2/x]t_1'\).
  • If \(t_1 =_{\beta} t_1'\) and \(t_2 =_{\beta} t_2'\), then \(t_1 t_2 =_{\beta} t_1' t_2'\).
  • If \(t_1 =_{\beta} t_1'\), then \(\lambda x.t_1 =_{\beta} \lambda x.t_1'\).

docs.title: \(\eta\)-Conversion
docs.text:
• \(\forall x\) and \(\forall term\ t'\), \(\lambda y.(\lambda x.t')y =_{\eta} \lambda x.t'\)
  • if \(t_1 =_{\eta} t_1'\) and \(t_2 =_{\eta} t_2'\), then \(t_1 t_2 =_{\eta} t_1' t_2'\).
  • if \(t_1 =_{\eta} t_1'\), then \(\lambda x.t_1 =_{\eta} \lambda x.t_1'\).

docs.title: Function Composition
docs.text:
• composition operator: \(\circ\)
  • \((f \circ g )(x) = f(g(x))\)
  • \(f \circ g = \lambda x.f(g(x))\)
  • \(\circ\) itself is a function : \(\lambda f.\lambda g.\lambda x.f(g(x))\)

docs.title: Representing Natural Numbers
docs.text: \[ \begin{align*} &\bar{0} = \lambda s.\lambda z.z =z\\ &\bar{1} = \lambda s.\lambda z.s\ z\\ &\bar{2} = \lambda s.\lambda z.s\ (s\ z)\\ &\bar{3} = \lambda s.\lambda z.s\ (s\ (s\ z))\\ & ...\\ &\bar{n} = \lambda s.\lambda z.s^n\ z\\ \end{align*} \]

docs.title: Define z and s
docs.text:
• The representation \(\bar{n}\) iterates its first argument \(n\) times on its second argument.
\[ \bar{n}fx = f^b(x) \]
  • To define a successor function that satisfies succ \(\bar{n} = \overline{n+1}\), we need to define \(s\) and \(z\).
\[ \begin{align*} &zeor = \bar{0} = \lambda s.\lambda z.z\\ &succ = \lambda n.\overline{n+1} = \lambda n.\lambda s.\lambda z.s(n\ s\ z)\\ \end{align*} \]
  • To define addition, we need to define \(add\).
\[ \begin{align*} &add = \lambda m.\lambda n.m\ succ\ n\\ \end{align*} \]
  • To define multiplication, we need to define \(mul\).
\[ \begin{align*} &mul = λm. λn. λf. m (n f)\\ \end{align*} \]

Let's walk through a concrete example of the multiplication function in lambda calculus, using Church numerals to represent numbers. The Church numeral for a natural number \( n \) is defined as a function that applies a given function \( f \) to an argument \( x \), \( n \)-times. Here’s a quick refresher on the Church numerals:

  • 0: \( \lambda f. \lambda x. x \)
  • 1: \( \lambda f. \lambda x. f(x) \)
  • 2: \( \lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(x)) \)
  • 3: \( \lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(f(x))) \)
  • And so on.

Multiplication Function: The multiplication function is: [ mul = \lambda m.\lambda n.\lambda f. m (n f) ] This means \( m \) is applied \( n \)-times to a function \( f \).

Example: Multiply 2 and 3 To demonstrate, we'll compute \( 2 \times 3 \) using Church numerals for 2 and 3.

  • \( 2 \) is \( \lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(x)) \)
  • \( 3 \) is \( \lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(f(x))) \)

Now, let’s compute \( mul(2)(3) \):

  1. Apply \( mul \) to 2:
\[ \begin{align*} &mul\ 2 = \lambda n.\lambda f. 2 (n f)\\ &\text{Substituting } 2 = \lambda f.\lambda x.f(f(x)):\\ &mul\ 2 = \lambda n.\lambda f. (\lambda f.\lambda x. f(f(x))) (n f)\\ \end{align*} \]
  1. Apply \( mul(2) \) to 3:
\[ \begin{align*} &\text{Now,apply} n = 3 = \lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(f(x)))\\ &mul\ 2\ 3 = \lambda f. (\lambda x. f(f(x))) (3 f)\\ &\text{Substituting } 3 f = \lambda x. f(f(f(x))):\\ &mul\ 2\ 3 = \lambda f. (\lambda x. f(f(x))) (\lambda x. f(f(f(x))))\\ \end{align*} \]
  1. Simplify the Expression:
\[ \begin{align*} &\text{Now, apply } \lambda x. f(f(x)) \text{ to } \lambda x. f(f(f(x))), \text{ replacing } x \text{ in } f(f(x)) \text{ with } \lambda x. f(f(f(x))), \text{ resulting in:}\\ &mul\ 2\ 3 = \lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(f(f(f(f(x))))))\\ \end{align*} \]

Thus, \( mul\ 2\ 3 = \lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(f(f(f(f(x)))))) \), which is the Church numeral for 6.

Conclusion: This result shows that applying the multiplication function to the Church numerals for 2 and 3 correctly gives the Church numeral for 6, as expected.

  • To define exponentiation, we need to define \(exp\).
\[ \begin{align*} &exp = \lambda m.\lambda n.n\ m\\ \end{align*} \]

In lambda calculus, exponentiation (exp) can be defined as repeated application of multiplication. Specifically, exponentiation can be thought of as applying a number \( n \) (the exponent) to a function \( m \) (the base) a number of times. This means we can define exponentiation in terms of function application.

Explanation: - \( m \) is the base, which is a Church numeral. - \( n \) is the exponent, which is also a Church numeral. - In lambda calculus, \( n\ m \) means applying \( m \), \( n \)-times. Since a Church numeral represents the number of times to apply a function, this effectively results in exponentiation.

This function takes two Church numerals \( m \) and \( n \), and applies the base \( m \), \( n \)-times. The result is \( m^n \), which is the Church numeral representing the result of exponentiation.

Example: \( 2^3 \) Let’s compute \( 2^3 \) using this definition.

  1. Church Numerals: - \( 2 = \lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(x)) \) - \( 3 = \lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(f(x))) \)

  2. Exponentiation Function:

\[ \begin{align*} &exp = \lambda m. \lambda n. n\ m\\ \end{align*} \]
  1. Apply \( exp \) to \( 2 \) and \( 3 \):
\[ \begin{align*} &exp\ 2\ 3 = 3\ 2\\ &\text{Substituting } 3 = \lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(f(x)))\\ &\text{this becomes:}\\ &exp\ 2\ 3 = (\lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(f(x))))\ 2\\ \end{align*} \]
  1. Simplification:
\[ \begin{align*} &\text{Now, apply } 2 = \lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(x)) \text{ to } 3 = \lambda f. \lambda x. f(f(f(x))), \text{ resulting in:}\\ &exp\ 2\ 3 = \lambda x. 2(2(2(x)))\\ \end{align*} \]

Expanding this, each application of \( 2 \) adds another layer of function application:

\[ \begin{align*} &= \lambda x. 2(2(f(f(x)))\\ &= \lambda x. 2(f(f(f(f(x))))\\ &= \lambda x. f(f(f(f(f(f(f(f(x)))))))\\ \end{align*} \]

This result corresponds to the Church numeral for \( 8 \), which is \( 2^3 \).

docs.text:

4.二项分布

  • \(b(k,n,p)=b(n-k,n,1-p)\)
  • \(\frac{b(k,n,p)}{b(k-1,n,p)}=1+\frac{(n+1)p-k}{kq}\)
  • \((n+1)p\)是整数 ： \((n+1)p \ (n+1)p-1\) 为最有可能的成功次数
  • \((n+1)p\)是不整数： \(k=[(n+1)p]\) 最有可能的成功次数 \([x]\)表示\(x\)最大整数部分
  • 递推公式 \(P(\epsilon=k+1)=\frac{p(n-k)}{(k+1)q}P(\epsilon=k)\)
  • \(n \rightarrow +\infty\) 「泊松定理」

若存在正常数\(\lambda\) 当\(n \rightarrow+\infty\)时，有\(bp_n \rightarrow +\lambda\) ,则

\(lim_{n \rightarrow+\infty} b(k,n,p)=\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}e^{-\lambda}\)

通常，n与p无关，但是n很大，p很小，np不是很大的时候，可近似地取\(\lambda=np\)

  • 德莫佛-拉普拉斯定理 \(npq \rightarrow +\infty\)

\(\begin{align*}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-\frac{(t-a)^2}{2\sigma^2}}dt)^2 &= (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-\frac{t^2}{2}}dt)^2\\&=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{\frac{t^2+s^2}{2}}dtds\\ &=\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta\int_{0}^{+\infty} re^{-\frac{r^2}{2}}dr\\ &=1\end{align*}\)

Conclusion

\(\Sigma^{'} = JW\Sigma W^TJ^T\) where W is a view transformation and J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation

Derivation

docs.title: The viewing transformation:
docs.text:
Denote the Gaussian reconstruction kernels in object space by \(r_{k}''(\mathbf{t})=\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V''}}(\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{t_k})\), where \(\mathbf{t_k}\) are the voxel positions of center of kernel.

Denote camera coordinates by a vector \(\mathbf{u}=(u_0,u_1,u_2)^{T}\). Object coordinates are transformed to camera coordinates using an afﬁne mapping \(\mathbf{u}=\varphi(\mathbf{t})=\mathbf{Wt+d}\), called viewing tranformation.

Now we can transform the reconstruction kernels \(\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V''}}(\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{t_k})\) to camera space:

\(\(\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V''}}(\varphi^{-1}(\mathbf{u})-\mathbf{t_k})=\frac{1}{|\mathbf{W}^{-1}|}\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V'}_{k}}(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u_k})=r_{k}'(\mathbf{u})\)\)

where \(\mathbf{u_k}=\varphi(\mathbf{t_k})\) is the center of the Gaussian in camera coordinates and \(\mathbf{V'}_{k}=\mathbf{W}\mathbf{V''}_{k}\mathbf{W}^{T}\) is the variance matrix in camera coordinates.

docs.title: The Projective Transformation
docs.text:
In camera space, The ray intersecting the center of projection and the point \((x_0, x_1)\) on the projection plane is called a viewing ray.

To facilitate analiytical integration of volumn function, we need to transform the camera space to ray space such that the viewing rays are parallel to a coordinate axis. The projective transformation converts camera coordinates to ray coordinates.

Camera space is deﬁned such that the origin of the camera coordinate system is at the center of projection and the projection plane is the plane \(u_{2}=1\). Camera space and ray space are related by the mapping \(\mathbf{x=m(u)}\).

\[ \begin{pmatrix} x_0\\ x_1\\ x_2\\ \end{pmatrix} =\mathbf{m(u)}= \begin{pmatrix} u_{0}/u_{2}\\ u_{1}/u_{2}\\ \Vert(u_{0},u_{1},u_{2})^{T}\Vert\\ \end{pmatrix}\\\\ ~\\\\ \begin{pmatrix} u_0\\ u_1\\ u_2\\ \end{pmatrix} =\mathbf{m^{-1}(u)}= \begin{pmatrix} x_{0}/l\cdot x_2\\ x_{1}/l\cdot x_2\\ 1/l\cdot x_2\\ \end{pmatrix} \]

where \(l=\Vert(x_{0},x_{1},1)^{T}\Vert\).

Unfortunately, these mappings are not affine. The Gaussian after the transformation may not still Gaussian. To solve this problem, we introduce the local affine approximation \(m_{uk}\) of the projective transformation. It is defined by the first two terms of the Taylor expansion of \(\mathbf{m}\) at the point \(\mathbf{u}_k\):

\[ \mathbf{m_{u_k}(u)=x_k+J_{u_k}\cdot (u-u_k)}\\\\ ~\\ \mathbf{J_{u_k}}={\frac{\partial \mathbf{m}}{\partial \mathbf{u}}}(\mathbf{u}_k) \]

where \(\mathbf{x}_k=\mathbf{m(u_k)}\) is the center of a Gaussian in ray space and the Jacobian \(\mathbf{J_{u_k}}\) is given by the partial derivatives of \(\mathbf{m}\) at the point \(\mathbf{u}_k\).

This yields the local affine approximation of reconstruction kernels to ray space:

\[ \begin{aligned} r_{k}(\mathbf{x})&=\frac{1}{|\mathbf{W}^{-1}|}\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V'}_{k}}(\mathbf{m^{-1}(x)}-\mathbf{u_k})\\ &=\frac{1}{|\mathbf{W}^{-1}||\mathbf{J}^{-1}|}\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{V}_{k}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x_k}) \end{aligned} \]

where \(\mathbf{V}_k\) is the variance matrix in ray coordinates:

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{V}_{k}&=\mathbf{J}\mathbf{V'}_{k}\mathbf{J}^{T}\\ &=\mathbf{JW}\mathbf{V''}_{k}\mathbf{W}^{T}\mathbf{J}^{T} \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
1. 屏幕分割 : Split the screen into 16x16 tiles
  2. 视锥体裁剪 : 假设我们有一组3D高斯splat，每个splat代表一个体积数据点。首先，我们需要检查这些splat是否与视锥体相交:

Only keep the splats that have 99% confidence of intersecting the view frustum.

例如，如果有一个splat的中心位于视锥体之外，我们就不会考虑它。

  1. Use guard band to trivially reject splats that are at extreme positions : computing their 2D variance would be unstable.
  2. 实例化和排序

  • 假设一个splat与5个瓦片相交，我们为这个splat创建5个实例

  • 每个实例根据其在视空间中的深度和瓦片ID获得一个唯一的键

  • 使用GPU Radix排序算法，我们根据这些键对所有实例进行排序 5. Rasterization

  • 对于每个瓦片，我们确定排序后第一个和最后一个影响该瓦片的splat实例

  • 假设瓦片(5,5)首先加载了影响它的splat实例列表到共享内存

  • 对于瓦片(5,5)中的像素(5,5)，我们从列表的开始到结束遍历splat实例，累积颜色和α值

  • 当像素(5,5)的α值达到1时，我们知道它已经饱和，不再需要更多的splat实例来影响它的颜色

docs.text:
The image intensity at pixel \((u, v)\) and time \(t\) is computed as:

\[\mathbb{I}(u, v, t) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} p_i(u, v, t) \cdot \alpha_i \cdot c_i(\mathbf{d}) \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - p_j(u, v, t) \cdot \alpha_j)\]

Key Factorization

The 4D Gaussian probability can be factorized as:

\[p_i(u, v, t) = p_i(u, v | t) \cdot p_i(t)\]
  • Conditional 3D Gaussian: \(p_i(u, v | t)\) — spatial distribution at time \(t\)
  • Marginal 1D Gaussian: \(p_i(t)\) — temporal distribution

docs.title: Covariance Decomposition
docs.text:
Similar to 3D Gaussian Splatting, the 4D covariance matrix is decomposed as:

\[\Sigma = R S S^T R^T\]

Where:

Component Description Parameters \(S\) Scaling matrix \(\text{diag}(s_x, s_y, s_z, s_t)\) \(R\) Rotation matrix Two quaternions \(q_l, q_r\) \(\mu\) Mean position \((x, y, z, t)\)

docs.title: 4D Rotation via Quaternions
docs.text:
Isoclinic Decomposition

A 4D rotation can be decomposed into two isoclinic rotations, each represented by a quaternion:

\[R = L(q_l) \cdot R(q_r)\]

Left Quaternion Matrix \(L(q_l)\) where \(q_l = (a, b, c, d)\):

\[L(q_l) = \begin{pmatrix} a & -b & -c & -d \\ b & a & -d & c \\ c & d & a & -b \\ d & -c & b & a \end{pmatrix}\]

Right Quaternion Matrix \(R(q_r)\) where \(q_r = (p, q, r, s)\):

\[R(q_r) = \begin{pmatrix} p & -q & -r & -s \\ q & p & s & -r \\ r & -s & p & q \\ s & r & -q & p \end{pmatrix}\]

docs.title: Deriving the Conditional 3D Gaussian
docs.text:
Given the 4D covariance partitioned as:

\[\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_{xyz} & \Sigma_{xyz,t} \\ \Sigma_{xyz,t}^T & \Sigma_t \end{pmatrix}\]

The conditional 3D Gaussian (spatial distribution at time \(t\)):

\[\Sigma_{xyz|t} = \Sigma_{xyz} - \Sigma_{xyz,t} \Sigma_t^{-1} \Sigma_{xyz,t}^T\] \[\mu_{xyz|t} = \mu_{xyz} + \Sigma_{xyz,t} \Sigma_t^{-1} (t - \mu_t)\]

docs.title: Marginal 1D Gaussian
docs.text:
The temporal distribution is simply:

\[p(t) = \mathcal{N}(t; \mu_t, \Sigma_t)\]

docs.title: Background: Spherical Harmonics
docs.text:
What are Spherical Harmonics?

Orthogonal functions on the sphere surface, used to represent view-dependent appearance:

\[f(\theta, \phi) \approx \sum_l \sum_{m=-l}^{l} c_l^m Y_l^m(\theta, \phi)\]

Definition:

\[Y_l^m(\theta, \phi) = \sqrt{\frac{(2l+1)(l-m)!}{4\pi(l+m)!}} P_l^m(\cos\theta) e^{im\phi}\]

Where:

  • \(l\) — degree (non-negative integer)
  • \(m\) — order (\(-l \leq m \leq l\))
  • \(P_l^m\) — associated Legendre polynomials
  • \(c_l^m\) — SH coefficients

docs.title: Extension to 4D
docs.text:
4D Spherindrical Harmonics

To handle time-varying appearance, spherical harmonics are extended with a temporal component:

\[Z_{nl}^m(t, \theta, \phi) = \cos\left(\frac{2\pi n t}{T}\right) Y_l^m(\theta, \phi)\]

This allows modeling periodic color changes over time.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Aspect 3D-GS 4D-GS Scene type Static Dynamic Gaussian dimension 3D 4D (space + time) Rotation 1 quaternion 2 quaternions View-dependent color Spherical Harmonics Spherindrical Harmonics Real-time rendering ✅ ✅

docs.text:
Further Reading

  • Spherical Harmonics Introduction (Chinese)
  • Spherical Harmonics Deep Dive (Chinese)

docs.title: DDIM: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models
docs.text:
Paper Overview

Title: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models Authors: Jiaming Song, Chenlin Meng, Stefano Ermon Venue: ICLR 2021 Key Contribution: Enables much faster sampling (10-50× speedup) by making the reverse process deterministic and non-Markovian.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Problem with DDPM

DDPM requires hundreds to thousands of sequential denoising steps to generate a single image, making it computationally expensive for practical applications.

DDIM Solution: Reformulate the reverse process to allow for:

  • Deterministic sampling (same noise → same output)
  • Skipping timesteps during generation
  • Faster inference without retraining

docs.title: Non-Markovian Reverse Process
docs.text:
Unlike DDPM's stochastic Markovian process, DDIM uses a deterministic reverse process:

\[x_{t-1} = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}} \underbrace{\left( \frac{x_t - \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t} \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}} \right)}_{\text{predicted } x_0} + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_{t-1}} \cdot \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\]

Advantages

Feature DDPM DDIM Sampling Stochastic Deterministic Steps needed ~1000 ~50-100 Same noise → same image ❌ ✅ Interpolation in latent space ❌ ✅

docs.title: Accelerated Sampling
docs.text:
DDIM allows using a subsequence of timesteps \(\{\tau_1, \tau_2, \ldots, \tau_S\}\) where \(S \ll T\):

Result

  • Original DDPM: 1000 steps
  • DDIM: 50-100 steps with comparable quality
  • 10-50× speedup in generation time

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Further Reading

  • DDIM Explained (Chinese) - Detailed derivation and intuition
  • Original Paper - arXiv preprint

docs.title: DDPM: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
docs.text:
Paper Overview

Title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models Authors: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain, Pieter Abbeel Venue: NeurIPS 2020 Key Contribution: Established the mathematical foundation for diffusion-based generative models that achieve high-quality image synthesis.

docs.title: Forward Diffusion Process
docs.text:
The forward process gradually adds Gaussian noise to data over \(T\) timesteps, defined as a Markov chain:

\[q(x_1, \ldots, x_T | x_0) = \prod_{t=1}^T q(x_t | x_{t-1})\]

where each transition is:

\[q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}(x_t; \sqrt{1-\beta_t} x_{t-1}, \beta_t I)\]

Sampling at Time \(t\)

We can sample \(x_t\) directly from \(x_0\) without computing all intermediate steps:

\[x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t} \epsilon\]

where \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\)

Key Notation:

Symbol Definition \(\alpha_t\) \(1 - \beta_t\) \(\bar{\alpha}_t\) \(\prod_{i=1}^t \alpha_i\) (cumulative product) \(\beta_t\) Noise schedule at timestep \(t\)

docs.title: Reverse Diffusion Process
docs.text:
The reverse process learns to denoise, parameterized by a neural network that predicts the noise:

Training Objective

The model is trained using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), optimizing the variational lower bound (ELBO) of the log-likelihood.

After mathematical derivation, the simplified objective becomes:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, \epsilon} \left[ \| \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) \|^2 \right]\]

Key Insight

The neural network \(\epsilon_\theta\) learns to predict the noise \(\epsilon\) that was added to create \(x_t\) from \(x_0\).

docs.title: Noise Schedule
docs.text:
The noise schedule \(\{\beta_t\}_{t=1}^T\) controls how quickly information is destroyed:

  • Linear schedule: \(\beta_t\) increases linearly from \(\beta_1 = 10^{-4}\) to \(\beta_T = 0.02\)
  • Cosine schedule: Provides more gradual noise addition (proposed in improved DDPM)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Further Reading

  1. What are Diffusion Models? - Lilian Weng's comprehensive blog post
  2. An In-Depth Guide to DDPM - Theory to Implementation
  3. DDPM Explained (YouTube) - Video explanation

docs.title: Stable Diffusion: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models
docs.text:
Paper Overview

Title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models Authors: Robin Rombach, Andreas Blattmann, Dominik Lorenz, Patrick Esser, Björn Ommer Venue: CVPR 2022 Key Contribution: Performs diffusion in a compressed latent space, dramatically reducing computational cost while enabling high-resolution synthesis and flexible conditioning.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The model consists of three main components:

graph LR
    A[Image x] --> B[Encoder ε]
    B --> C[Latent z]
    C --> D[Diffusion in Latent Space]
    D --> E[Decoder D]
    E --> F[Output x̂]

docs.title: 1. Perceptual Image Compression
docs.text:
Autoencoder

The autoencoder compresses images to a lower-dimensional latent space:

Component Function Dimensions Encoder \(\mathcal{E}\) \(x \rightarrow z\) \(\mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{h \times w \times c}\) Decoder \(\mathcal{D}\) \(z \rightarrow \hat{x}\) \(\mathbb{R}^{h \times w \times c} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}\)

Regularization Options:

  • KL-regularization: Slight KL penalty towards standard normal
  • VQ-regularization: Vector quantization within the decoder

Compression Ratio

Typical compression factor: 8× (e.g., 512×512 → 64×64 latent)

docs.title: 2. Latent Diffusion Model
docs.text:
The diffusion process operates in the compressed latent space using a time-conditioned U-Net:

\[\mathcal{L}_{LDM} = \mathbb{E}_{z, \epsilon, t} \left[ \| \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(z_t, t) \|^2 \right]\]

Advantages over Pixel-Space Diffusion

  • ~64× fewer pixels to process
  • Faster training and inference
  • Perceptually equivalent quality

docs.title: 3. Conditioning Mechanisms
docs.text:
For conditional generation, the model uses cross-attention:

Cross-Attention Mechanism

\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d}}\right) V\]

Where:

  • \(Q = W_Q \cdot \phi(z_t)\) — Query from U-Net features
  • \(K = W_K \cdot \tau_\theta(y)\) — Key from condition encoder
  • \(V = W_V \cdot \tau_\theta(y)\) — Value from condition encoder

Condition Encoder \(\tau_\theta\):

Modality Encoder Type Text prompts CLIP / BERT Images CNN / ViT Semantic maps Spatial encoder

Joint Training

Both \(\tau_\theta\) (condition encoder) and \(\epsilon_\theta\) (U-Net) are trained jointly, enabling flexible multi-modal conditioning.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Aspect Description Innovation Diffusion in latent space Compression 8× spatial reduction Conditioning Cross-attention mechanism Applications Text-to-image, inpainting, super-resolution

docs.title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
docs.text:
Paper Overview

Title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis Authors: Ben Mildenhall, Pratul P. Srinivasan, Matthew Tancik, et al. Venue: ECCV 2020 (Best Paper Honorable Mention) Key Contribution: Represents 3D scenes as continuous neural radiance fields, enabling photorealistic novel view synthesis from sparse input images.

docs.title: Core Idea
docs.text:
Key Insight

Overfit a single MLP to represent one specific scene. The network learns a continuous volumetric representation that maps 3D coordinates to color and density.

Input/Output:

Input Output 3D position \((x, y, z)\) Volume density \(\sigma\) Viewing direction \((\theta, \phi)\) RGB color \((r, g, b)\)

docs.title: Rendering Process
docs.text:
1. Sample 5D coordinates along camera rays
  2. Query MLP to get color and density at each point
  3. Composite values using volume rendering
  4. Optimize by minimizing reconstruction loss

docs.title: Network Architecture
docs.text:
MLP Structure

The network \(F_\Theta\) processes inputs as follows:

  1. Input: 3D coordinate \((x, y, z)\)
  2. 8 fully-connected layers (ReLU, 256 channels)
  3. Output: Density \(\sigma\) + 256-dim feature vector
  4. Concatenate feature with viewing direction \((\theta, \phi)\)
  5. 1 additional FC layer (ReLU, 128 channels)
  6. Output: View-dependent RGB color

Design Choice

  • Density \(\sigma\) depends only on position → multiview consistent geometry
  • Color depends on both position and direction → view-dependent effects (specular highlights)

docs.title: Mathematical Formulation
docs.text:
The expected color \(C(\mathbf{r})\) along ray \(\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}\) is:

\[C(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{t_n}^{t_f} T(t) \cdot \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}) \, dt\]

Where transmittance \(T(t)\) represents the probability of the ray traveling from \(t_n\) to \(t\) without hitting anything:

\[T(t) = \exp\left(-\int_{t_n}^{t} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) \, ds\right)\]

docs.title: Discrete Approximation
docs.text:
Using quadrature with \(N\) samples:

\[\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} T_i \cdot \alpha_i \cdot \mathbf{c}_i\]

where \(\alpha_i = 1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i)\) and \(T_i = \prod_{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alpha_j)\)

docs.title: 1. Positional Encoding
docs.text:
Problem

MLPs struggle to learn high-frequency functions directly from low-dimensional inputs.

Solution: Map inputs to higher-dimensional space using sinusoidal functions:

\[\gamma(p) = \left( \sin(2^0\pi p), \cos(2^0\pi p), \ldots, \sin(2^{L-1}\pi p), \cos(2^{L-1}\pi p) \right)\]

docs.title: 2. Hierarchical Volume Sampling
docs.text:
Efficiency Improvement

Use two networks to focus samples where matter exists:

Network Purpose Samples Coarse Identify relevant regions \(N_c\) uniform samples Fine Detailed rendering \(N_f\) importance-sampled

Process:

  1. Run coarse network with uniform samples
  2. Compute weights \(w_i = T_i \alpha_i\) from coarse output
  3. Sample \(N_f\) additional points proportional to weights
  4. Run fine network with all \(N_c + N_f\) samples

At Test Time

Only the fine network is used for final rendering.

docs.title: Training Details
docs.text: Parameter Value Coarse samples (\(N_c\)) 64 Fine samples (\(N_f\)) 128 Batch size 4096 rays Iterations 100-300K Positional encoding (position) \(L = 10\) Positional encoding (direction) \(L = 4\)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Takeaway

"The weight is the scene" — NeRF encodes an entire 3D scene within the weights of a single neural network.
