docs.title: 📐 Foundations: MDP & Core Concepts
docs.text:
The Basic Vocabulary of Reinforcement Learning

Prerequisites: Linear algebra, probability, basic calculus

docs.title: 🎯 The Markov Decision Process (MDP)
docs.text:
One sentence

An MDP defines a sequential decision-making problem where an agent interacts with an environment.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
An MDP is a tuple \((\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, R, \gamma)\):

Symbol Name Description Example \(\mathcal{S}\) State space All possible situations Robot joint angles, game pixels \(\mathcal{A}\) Action space All possible decisions Motor torques, button presses \(P(s'\|s,a)\) Transition dynamics Probability of next state Physics simulation, game rules \(R(s,a,s')\) Reward function Immediate reward Score, distance to goal \(\gamma \in [0,1]\) Discount factor Future reward weight 0.99 (care about future)

docs.title: The Markov Property
docs.text:
Key insight

The future depends only on the current state, not the history.

\[ P(s_{t+1}|s_t, a_t) = P(s_{t+1}|s_0, a_0, \ldots, s_t, a_t) \]

This means we don't need to remember the entire trajectory to predict what happens next.

docs.title: The Goal
docs.text:
Find a policy \(\pi(a|s)\) that maximizes expected cumulative reward:

\[ J(\pi) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t r_t\right] \]

docs.title: ⚖️ Exploration vs. Exploitation
docs.text:
The dilemma: Should we try new actions (explore) or stick with what works (exploit)?

Strategy Description Exploitation Use current knowledge to get high rewards Exploration Try new actions to gain information ε-greedy With probability ε, take random action Entropy bonus Add \(-\beta \log \pi(a\|s)\) to keep policy spread out

Why it matters

Without exploration, the agent might never discover better strategies. With too much exploration, it wastes time on bad actions.

docs.title: Policy, Value, and Q-Functions
docs.text:
Policy \(\pi(a|s)\): A distribution over actions given a state.

Value function \(V^\pi(s)\): Expected total reward starting from state \(s\):

\[ V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\left[\sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t r_t \mid s_0 = s\right] \]

Q-function \(Q^\pi(s,a)\): Expected total reward starting from \(s\), taking action \(a\):

\[ Q^\pi(s,a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\left[\sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t r_t \mid s_0 = s, a_0 = a\right] \]

Advantage \(A^\pi(s,a)\): How much better is action \(a\) than average?

\[ A^\pi(s,a) = Q^\pi(s,a) - V^\pi(s) \]

Interpretation

If \(A^\pi(s,a) > 0\), action \(a\) is better than average; if \(A^\pi(s,a) < 0\), it's worse.

docs.title: Bellman Equations
docs.text:
Bellman equation for \(V^\pi\) (recursive definition):

\[ V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi, s' \sim P}\left[r(s,a,s') + \gamma V^\pi(s')\right] \]

Intuition

"The value of a state is the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state."

Bellman optimality equation (for the best possible policy):

\[ V^*(s) = \max_a \mathbb{E}_{s' \sim P}\left[r(s,a,s') + \gamma V^*(s')\right] \] \[ Q^*(s,a) = \mathbb{E}_{s' \sim P}\left[r(s,a,s') + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^*(s',a')\right] \]

Key Takeaway

These equations are the foundation of Q-learning and all value-based methods.

docs.title: 📊 Q-Learning (Tabular Methods)
docs.text: The foundation of value-based RL

docs.title: The Problem & Solution
docs.text: Problem How do we learn without a teacher? Solution The Bellman Equation Key Idea Bootstrap from future values

docs.title: Visual: Q-Learning in Action
docs.text:
Interactive Animation

The animation below shows Q-learning step by step:

docs.title: The Q-Table Structure
docs.text:
The Q-table is essentially a spreadsheet:

  • Rows: Every possible state \(s\) (e.g., grid coordinates \((i, j)\))
  • Columns: Every possible action \(a\) (Up, Down, Left, Right)
  • Cells: The value \(Q(s,a)\) = expected future reward

docs.title: The Math
docs.text:
Bellman optimality (definition of \(Q^*\)):

\[ Q^*(s,a) = \mathbb{E}\left[ r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^*(s', a') \right] \]

Q-learning update (how we learn it):

\[ Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha \left[ r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s,a) \right] \] Parameter Meaning Typical Value \(\alpha\) Learning rate 0.1 \(\gamma\) Discount factor 0.99

Limitation

Curse of dimensionality. With 7 joints and 100 angles each, the table has \(100^7\) entries. You run out of RAM.

Key Takeaway

Q-learning works for small state spaces but fails with high dimensions. The table has \(|\mathcal{S}| \times |\mathcal{A}|\) entries.

docs.title: 🎭 Policy Gradient & Actor-Critic
docs.text: From learning values to learning policies

docs.title: Value-Based vs. Policy-Based
docs.text: Approach Method Example Value-Based Learn \(Q(s,a)\), act greedily Q-learning, DQN Policy-Based Learn \(\pi_\theta(a\|s)\) directly REINFORCE, PPO

docs.title: REINFORCE (Monte Carlo Policy Gradient)
docs.text:
REINFORCE improves a policy by running an episode, looking at total reward from each step (\(G_t\)), and making high-reward actions more likely.

The Return (Reward-to-Go)

\[G_t = r_t + \gamma r_{t+1} + \gamma^2 r_{t+2} + \cdots\]

So \(G_t\) is the discounted sum of all rewards from step \(t\) until the end.

REINFORCE update:

\[ \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha \sum_t G_t \, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t | s_t) \]

Intuition

  • If \(G_t\) is large → push \(\theta\) to make \(\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\) larger
  • If \(G_t\) is small → push \(\theta\) to make \(\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\) smaller

Variance reduction with baseline:

\[ \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha \sum_t (G_t - b(s_t)) \, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t | s_t) \] Why is there a log? (Derivation)

See The Policy Gradient Theorem and its Derivation

docs.title: Actor-Critic
docs.text:
In one sentence

Actor-Critic = REINFORCE + a Critic network that estimates "how good is this state?" reducing variance and stabilizing learning.

Component Role What it does Actor \(\pi_\theta(a\|s)\) Policy Chooses actions Critic \(V_\phi(s)\) Value estimator Provides baseline

Advantage calculation (TD error):

\[ A_t = r_t + \gamma V_\phi(s_{t+1}) - V_\phi(s_t) = \delta_t \]

Actor update:

\[ \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha \sum_t A_t \, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t | s_t) \]

Critic update (TD loss):

\[ \mathcal{L}(\phi) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \big( V_\phi(s_t) - (r_t + \gamma V_\phi(s_{t+1})) \big)^2 \right] \]

Key Takeaway

Policy gradients allow us to handle continuous action spaces and learn stochastic policies, unlike value-based methods.

docs.title: 🚀 DQN & DDPG (Deep RL)
docs.text: Neural Networks Meet RL

docs.title: The Problem & Solution
docs.text: Problem Can't store tables for high-dimensional inputs (pixels, joint angles) Solution Use neural networks to approximate \(Q(s,a)\)

docs.title: DQN (Deep Q-Network)
docs.text:
In one sentence

DQN is Q-learning with a neural network instead of a table, using a target network and experience replay to stabilize learning.

What is \(Q_\theta(s)\)?

The network takes state \(s\) as input and outputs a Q-value for each action:

\[ Q_\theta(s) \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}|} \]

TD target (what we want to learn):

\[ y = r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q_{\theta^-}(s', a') \]

Loss function:

\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(s,a,r,s')\sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \big( Q_\theta(s,a) - y \big)^2 \right] \]

Key Innovations

Innovation Why it helps Target network \(\theta^-\) Stabilizes target (updated every \(C\) steps) Experience replay \(\mathcal{D}\) Breaks temporal correlation, reuses data

docs.title: DDPG (Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient)
docs.text:
Why DQN doesn't work for robotics

DQN is for discrete actions. Robots need continuous actions (e.g. torque).

Architecture: Actor–Critic

Component Output Purpose Actor \(\pi_\phi(s)\) Continuous action \(a \in \mathbb{R}^d\) Policy Critic \(Q_ heta(s,a)\) Q-value Evaluation

Critic loss (TD):

\[ \mathcal{L}_Q( heta) = \mathbb{E}\left[ ig( Q_ heta(s,a) - (r + \gamma Q_{ heta^-}(s', \pi_{\phi^-}(s'))) ig)^2 ight] \]

Actor gradient (maximize critic):

\[ abla_\phi J(\phi) = \mathbb{E}_{s\sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ abla_a Q_ heta(s,a) ig|_{a=\pi_\phi(s)} abla_\phi \pi_\phi(s) ight] \]

Key Takeaway

Deep Q-learning combines tabular RL with function approximation. Target networks and experience replay stabilize training.

docs.title: ⚡ PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization)
docs.text: A reliable and widely-used algorithm

docs.title: The Problem & Solution
docs.text: Problem DQN/DDPG are brittle → small learning rate changes cause collapse Solution Clip the policy update to stay close to old policy

docs.title: Probability Ratio
docs.text:
\[ r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)} \]

Interpretation

  • \(r_t = 1\): No change in action probability
  • \(r_t > 1\): Action now more likely
  • \(r_t < 1\): Action now less likely

docs.title: The Clipped Surrogate Objective
docs.text:
PPO's Key Innovation

\[\mathcal{L}^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t \left[ \min\big( r_t(\theta) \hat{A}_t,\; \text{clip}(r_t(\theta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) \hat{A}_t \big) \right]\] Advantage Ratio change Effect \(\hat{A}_t > 0\) (good) \(r_t\) increases Clipped if \(r_t > 1+\epsilon\) \(\hat{A}_t < 0\) (bad) \(r_t\) decreases Clipped if \(r_t < 1-\epsilon\)

Typically \(\epsilon = 0.2\).

docs.title: Full PPO Loss
docs.text:
\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t \left[ -\mathcal{L}^{\text{CLIP}}_t + c_1 (V_\theta(s_t) - V^{\text{targ}}_t)^2 - c_2 \, H(\pi_\theta(\cdot|s_t)) \right] \] Term Purpose \(-\mathcal{L}^{\text{CLIP}}_t\) Policy improvement \(c_1 (V - V^{\text{targ}})^2\) Value function loss \(-c_2 H(\pi)\) Entropy bonus (exploration)

Why entropy?

High entropy = more exploration. The entropy bonus prevents the policy from becoming too deterministic too quickly.

docs.title: GAE (Generalized Advantage Estimation)
docs.text:
Visual: GAE Calculation

The animation below shows how GAE computes advantages backward through time:

GAE formula:

\[ \hat{A}_t = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} (\gamma \lambda)^l \delta_{t+l} \]

where \(\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\) is the TD error.

Key Takeaway

PPO's clipped objective prevents destructive policy updates, enabling multiple epochs on the same batch. This makes it sample-efficient and stable.

docs.title: 🌐 Modern Applications
docs.text: Specialized variants for different domains

docs.title: 🤖 Robotics: Teacher–Student Distillation
docs.text:
Problem Simulation is perfect, reality is noisy; policies trained in sim often fail in real world Solution Train Teacher with privileged info, then distill to Student

1. Teacher (privileged policy) \(\pi_T(a \mid s, p)\)

  • Input: state \(s\) + privileged info \(p\) (friction, terrain)
  • Trained with PPO in simulation

2. Student (sensorimotor policy) \(\pi_S(a \mid s)\)

  • Input: only \(s\) (sensors only, no privileged \(p\))
  • Loss: supervised mimicry:
\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{BC}} = \mathbb{E}_{(s,p)\sim \text{sim}} \left[ \big\| \pi_S(s) - \pi_T(s, p) \big\|^2 \right] \]

Why this works

The student is forced to infer hidden variables (terrain, friction) from sensor history alone, making it robust to sim-to-real gap.

docs.title: 🖥️ LLMs: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization)
docs.text:
Problem PPO needs a Critic. For 70B LLM, adding another 70B Critic is infeasible Solution GRPO — no Critic; use group of samples as baseline

Process:

  1. Prompt \(q\) (e.g., "Solve \(x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0\)")
  2. Sample \(G\) outputs \(\{o_1, \ldots, o_G\}\)
  3. Score each with reward \(r_i\)

Group advantage:

\[ \hat{A}_i = \frac{r_i - \mu_{\text{group}}}{\sigma_{\text{group}} + \epsilon} \]

Key Takeaway

GRPO removes the critic by using group statistics as a baseline. Perfect for LLMs where a separate 70B critic is infeasible.

docs.title: 🔬 SAC (Soft Actor-Critic)
docs.text:
Maximum Entropy + Experience Replay

Problem with PPO Throws away data after each update (on-policy). Not sample efficient. Solution Off-policy methods reuse old data via experience replay.

Paper: Haarnoja et al. (2018)

Maximum entropy objective:

\[ J(\pi) = \sum_{t=0}^\infty \mathbb{E}_{(s_t, a_t) \sim \pi} \left[r(s_t, a_t) + \alpha H(\pi(\cdot|s_t))\right] \]

Why high entropy?

More exploration → more robust policies

Components:

Component Purpose Twin Q-networks Combat overestimation Squashed Gaussian policy Bounded continuous actions Replay buffer Store and reuse experience Auto temperature Learn \(\alpha\) automatically

docs.title: SAC vs PPO
docs.text:
Aspect PPO SAC Data reuse No (on-policy) Yes (replay buffer) Sample efficiency Lower Higher Stability Very stable Can diverge

When to use SAC

Real robotics (expensive samples), continuous control benchmarks.

docs.title: 🏭 Offline RL
docs.text:
Learning from Fixed Datasets

Problem Online RL requires environment interaction. Can't use in healthcare, driving. Solution Learn from logged data only (no exploration).

docs.title: The Challenge: Extrapolation Error
docs.text:
Dataset actions: a₁, a₂, a₃ (Q is accurate here)
Q-learning picks: argmax_a Q(s,a) = a_new (not in dataset!)
Problem: Q(s, a_new) is unreliable → policy exploits errors

docs.title: Conservative Q-Learning (CQL)
docs.text:
Paper: Kumar et al. (2020)

Idea: Penalize Q-values on out-of-distribution actions.

\[ L_{CQL} = \alpha \left(\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[\log \sum_a \exp Q(s,a)\right] - \mathbb{E}_{(s,a) \sim \mathcal{D}}[Q(s,a)]\right) + L_{TD} \]

docs.title: Implicit Q-Learning (IQL)
docs.text:
Paper: Kostrikov et al. (2021)

Idea: Avoid the \(\max\) entirely via expectile regression.

Key Takeaway

Offline RL enables learning from logged data (healthcare, driving). CQL and IQL avoid extrapolation errors by being conservative.

docs.title: 🌍 Model-Based RL
docs.text:
Learning Dynamics to Plan Ahead

Problem Model-free RL is sample inefficient. Learns only from actual experience. Solution Learn a model of the environment, generate synthetic experience.

docs.title: The Model-Based Paradigm
docs.text:
Idea: Learn \(\hat{P}(s'|s,a)\) (dynamics model), then:

  1. Generate imaginary rollouts
  2. Train policy on real + synthetic data
  3. Achieve much better sample efficiency

Trade-off

Model error can hurt performance. Use short rollouts (k = 1-5 steps).

docs.title: MBPO (Model-Based Policy Optimization)
docs.text:
Paper: Janner et al. (2019)

Algorithm:

  1. Train dynamics model: \(\hat{P}(s'|s,a) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta(s,a), \Sigma_\theta(s,a))\)
  2. Generate k-step rollouts from real states
  3. Add synthetic transitions to replay buffer
  4. Train SAC on real + synthetic data

Result: 3-5x fewer samples than SAC alone!

docs.title: Dreamer: World Models
docs.text:
Paper: Hafner et al. (2020)

Idea: For image-based tasks, learn in latent space.

Component Function Encoder \(o_t \to z_t\) Latent dynamics \(z_{t+1} \sim P(z_{t+1}\|z_t, a_t)\) Decoder \(z_t \to \hat{o}_t\)

docs.title: When to Use Model-Based RL
docs.text:
✅ Use when ❌ Don't use when Samples are expensive Samples are cheap Short-horizon tasks Long-horizon tasks Smooth dynamics Discontinuous dynamics

Key Takeaway

Model-based RL achieves maximum sample efficiency by learning environment dynamics. Short rollouts (MBPO) or latent models (Dreamer) combat model error.

docs.title: 📝 Algorithm Summary
docs.text:
Algorithm Key Innovation Best For Q-Learning Bellman equation Small discrete REINFORCE/AC Policy gradients Continuous DQN/DDPG Neural networks High-dim states PPO Clipped objective General purpose GRPO Group baseline LLMs SAC Max entropy Sample efficiency CQL/IQL Conservative Q Offline data MBPO/Dreamer Learned dynamics Max efficiency

Related Notes

  • Policy Gradient Methods (Detailed)

docs.title: Policy Gradient Methods: From REINFORCE to PPO
docs.text:
Overview

This note covers the evolution of policy gradient methods in reinforcement learning, from the foundational REINFORCE algorithm to the state-of-the-art Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO).

docs.title: 1. Foundation: REINFORCE and Policy Gradient Theorem
docs.text: Policy Gradient (PG) methods directly parameterize the policy \(\pi_\theta(a|s)\) and optimize via gradient ascent on an objective function.

docs.title: 1.1 The Objective Function
docs.text:
Goal

Maximize the expected cumulative discounted reward:

\[J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}[R(\tau)] = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T \gamma^t R(s_t, a_t)\right]\]

where \(\tau = (s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1, \ldots)\) is a trajectory.

docs.title: 1.2 The Policy Gradient Theorem
docs.text:
Key Result

\[ abla_ heta J( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{ au \sim \pi_ heta}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a_t|s_t) \cdot R( au) ight]\] Derivation (Click to expand)

Step 1: Express as integral over trajectories

\[ abla_ heta J( heta) = abla_ heta \int P( au| heta) R( au) d au\]

Step 2: Apply log-derivative trick: \( abla f = f abla \log f\)

\[= \int P( au| heta) abla_ heta \log P( au| heta) R( au) d au\]

Step 3: Decompose trajectory probability

\[P( au| heta) = p(s_0) \prod_{t=0}^{T-1} \pi_ heta(a_t|s_t) p(s_{t+1}|s_t, a_t)\]

Step 4: Take gradient (environment dynamics vanish!)

\[ abla_ heta \log P( au| heta) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a_t|s_t)\]

Model-Free

The gradient does not depend on environment dynamics \(p(s_{t+1}|s_t, a_t)\) — this is what makes it model-free!

docs.title: 1.3 The REINFORCE Algorithm
docs.text:
Using causality (actions can't affect past rewards), we use return-from-time-\(t\):

\[G_t = \sum_{k=t}^T \gamma^{k-t} R_k\]

Gradient Estimator:

\[\hat{g}_{\text{REINFORCE}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=0}^T \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t^{(i)}|s_t^{(i)}) G_t^{(i)}\]

Limitation

Monte Carlo estimation of \(G_t\) has high variance, leading to unstable training.

docs.title: 2.1 The Actor and The Critic
docs.text: Component Role Parameters Actor \(\pi_\theta(a\|s)\) Policy (action selection) \(\theta\) Critic \(V_\phi(s)\) Value estimation \(\phi\)

docs.title: 2.2 The Advantage Function
docs.text:
Key Idea: Baseline Subtraction

Subtracting a baseline \(b(s)\) reduces variance without adding bias:

\[\mathbb{E}[ abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a|s) \cdot b(s)] = 0\]

Proof: \(\sum_a abla_ heta \pi_ heta(a|s) = abla_ heta(1) = 0\)

The Advantage Function:

\[A^\pi(s, a) = Q^\pi(s, a) - V^\pi(s)\]

Intuition

\(A(s,a) > 0\) means action \(a\) is better than average in state \(s\).

docs.title: 2.3 Actor-Critic Updates
docs.text:
Advantage Estimation (TD Error):

\[\hat{A}(s_t, a_t) = R_t + \gamma V_\phi(s_{t+1}) - V_\phi(s_t)\]

Actor Update (gradient ascent):

\[\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t|s_t) \hat{A}(s_t, a_t)\]

Critic Update (gradient descent):

\[\phi \leftarrow \phi - \beta \nabla_\phi \left(R_t + \gamma V_\phi(s_{t+1}) - V_\phi(s_t)\right)^2\]

docs.title: 3. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)
docs.text:
Problems with A2C

  • Sample inefficient: On-policy data can only be used once
  • Unstable: Large policy updates can be catastrophic

docs.title: 3.1 The Probability Ratio
docs.text:
\[r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t | s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t | s_t)}\]

Interpretation

  • \(r_t = 1\): No change in action probability
  • \(r_t > 1\): Action now more likely
  • \(r_t < 1\): Action now less likely

docs.title: 3.2 The Clipped Surrogate Objective
docs.text:
PPO's Key Innovation

\[L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t \left[ \min \left( r_t(\theta) A_t, \; \text{clip}(r_t(\theta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) A_t \right) \right]\]

How it works:

Advantage Ratio change Effect \(A_t > 0\) \(r_t\) increases Good! But clipped if \(r_t > 1+\epsilon\) \(A_t < 0\) \(r_t\) decreases Good! But clipped if \(r_t < 1-\epsilon\)

The min creates a pessimistic bound — we only take credit for improvements within the trust region.

docs.title: 3.3 Full PPO Objective
docs.text:
\[L^{\text{PPO}}(\theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_t \left[ L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) - c_1 L^{\text{VF}}(\phi) + c_2 S[\pi_\theta](s_t) \right]\] Term Purpose \(L^{\text{CLIP}}\) Policy improvement (clipped) \(L^{\text{VF}}\) Value function loss: \((V_\phi(s_t) - G_t)^2\) \(S[\pi_\theta]\) Entropy bonus (encourages exploration) \(c_1, c_2\) Hyperparameter weights

Why PPO Works

  • Multiple epochs on same data → sample efficient
  • Clipping prevents catastrophic updates → stable
  • Simple to implement → widely adopted

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Method Variance Sample Efficiency Stability REINFORCE High Low Low Actor-Critic Medium Low Medium PPO Low High High

docs.title: Finite Automata
docs.text:
Overview

This lecture introduces the fundamental concepts of Finite Automata and Regular Languages, which form the foundation of computational theory.

docs.title: Motivation Example
docs.text:
Given a weighted graph \(G\):

Problem Type Question Optimization What's the MST? What's the weight of the MST? Decision Does \(G\) have a spanning tree with weight at most \(k\)?

Key Insight: Decision Problems ↔ Languages

  • Decision Problem \(\Rightarrow\) A Language
  • Given a string \(w\), is \(w \in L = \{\text{encode}(G,k) \mid G \text{ is a graph with ST weight} \leq k\}\)?
  • Therefore: Decision Problem \(\Leftrightarrow\) Language

docs.title: Alphabet
docs.text:
Definition

An alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite set of symbols.

docs.title: String
docs.text:
Definition

A string is a finite sequence of symbols from an alphabet \(\Sigma\).

Operation Notation Description Concatenation \(w_1 w_2\) Join two strings Exponentiation \(w^n\) Repeat string \(n\) times Empty string \(\varepsilon\) String of length 0 Reverse \(w^R\) Reverse the string

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
Definition

A language is a set of strings over an alphabet \(\Sigma\).

Operations on Languages:

Operation Definition Concatenation \(L_1 L_2 = \{w_1 w_2 \mid w_1 \in L_1, w_2 \in L_2\}\) Exponentiation \(L^n = \{w^n \mid w \in L\}\) Kleene Star \(A^* = \bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty} A^i\) Kleene Plus \(A^+ = \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A^i\)

Important Distinction

  • \(\{\}\) has size 0 (empty set)
  • \(\{\varepsilon\}\) has size 1 (set containing empty string)

docs.title: Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA)
docs.text:
Definition

A Deterministic Finite Automaton is a 5-tuple \((K, \Sigma, \delta, s, F)\) where:

  • \(K\) — finite set of states
  • \(\Sigma\) — alphabet
  • \(\delta: K \times \Sigma \rightarrow K\) — transition function
  • \(s \in K\) — start state
  • \(F \subseteq K\) — set of accept states

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
A configuration of an FA is a pair \((q, w)\) where:

  • \(q \in K\) is the current state
  • \(w \in \Sigma^*\) is the remaining input

Transition Relations:

Notation Meaning \((q, w) \vdash_M (q', w')\) Yield in one step: \(w = aw'\) and \(\delta(q, a) = q'\) \((q, w) \vdash_M^* (q', w')\) Yield in zero or more steps

docs.title: Language Acceptance
docs.text:
Definition: M accepts language L

A DFA \(M\) accepts a language \(L\) if:

  1. \(M\) accepts all strings in \(L\)
  2. \(M\) rejects all strings not in \(L\)
\[L(M) = \{w \mid M \text{ accepts } w\}\]

Important: \(M\) accepts a unique language!

Regular Language

A language is regular if it is accepted by some finite automaton.

docs.title: Theorem: Closure under Union
docs.text:
Theorem

If \(A\) and \(B\) are regular languages, so is \(A \cup B\).

Proof (Product Construction)

Let \(M_A = (K_A, \Sigma, \delta_A, s_A, F_A)\) and \(M_B = (K_B, \Sigma, \delta_B, s_B, F_B)\) be DFAs accepting \(A\) and \(B\).

Construct \(M\) for \(A \cup B\):

Component Definition States \(K = K_A \times K_B\) Start \(s = (s_A, s_B)\) Accept \(F = (F_A \times K_B) \cup (K_A \times F_B)\) Transition \(\delta((q_A, q_B), a) = (\delta_A(q_A, a), \delta_B(q_B, a))\)

docs.title: Non-deterministic Finite Automata (NFA)
docs.text:
Key Differences from DFA

  • Next state is not uniquely determined
  • Allows \(\varepsilon\)-transitions: \(\delta(q, \varepsilon)\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A Non-deterministic Finite Automaton is a 5-tuple \((K, \Sigma, \Delta, s, F)\) where:

  • \(K\) — finite set of states
  • \(\Sigma\) — alphabet
  • \(\Delta \subseteq K \times (\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}) \times K\) — transition relation
  • \(s \in K\) — start state
  • \(F \subseteq K\) — accept states

docs.title: Acceptance
docs.text:
NFA Acceptance

\(M\) on input \(w\) accepts if \((s, w) \vdash_M^* (q, \varepsilon)\) for some \(q \in F\).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Construct NFA

Language: \(\{w \mid w \in \{a,b\}^*, \text{the second symbol from the end is } b\}\)

docs.title: NFA ↔ DFA Equivalence
docs.text:
Theorem

  • Given a NFA \(M\), there exists a DFA \(M'\) such that \(L(M) = L(M')\)
  • Given a DFA \(M\), there exists a NFA \(M'\) such that \(L(M) = L(M')\)

docs.title: Subset Construction (NFA → DFA)
docs.text:
Construction

Given NFA \(M = (K, \Sigma, \Delta, s, F)\), construct DFA \(M' = (K', \Sigma, \delta, s', F')\):

Component Definition \(K'\) \(2^K\) (power set of \(K\)) \(s'\) \(E(s)\) where \(E(q) = \{p \in K : (q, \varepsilon) \vdash_M^* (p, \varepsilon)\}\) \(F'\) \(\{Q \in K' \mid Q \cap F \neq \emptyset\}\) \(\delta(Q, a)\) \(\bigcup_{q \in Q} \bigcup_{p: (q,a,p) \in \Delta} E(p)\)

docs.title: Closure under Concatenation
docs.text:
Theorem

If \(A\) and \(B\) are regular languages, so is \(AB\).

Construction Details
  • \(K = K_A \cup K_B\)
  • \(s = s_A\)
  • \(F = F_B\)
  • Add \(\varepsilon\)-transitions from \(F_A\) to \(s_B\)

docs.title: Closure under Kleene Star
docs.text:
Theorem

If \(A\) is a regular language, so is \(A^*\).

Operation Construction \(A^+\) \(A^*\)

Summary

Concept Key Point DFA Deterministic, unique next state NFA Non-deterministic, multiple possible paths Regular Language Accepted by some FA NFA = DFA Same expressive power Closure Union, Concatenation, Kleene Star

docs.title: Space Complexity
docs.text:
Overview

This lecture explores space complexity—how much memory is needed to solve problems. We'll see the surprising result that PSPACE = NPSPACE and study hierarchy theorems.

docs.title: Space Usage
docs.text:
Definition

Machine Space \(S(n)\) DTM \(M\) Max tape cells used on any input of length \(n\) NTM \(N\) Max tape cells used on any branch for inputs of length \(n\)

docs.title: Space Complexity Classes
docs.text:
Key Classes

Class Definition PSPACE Decidable by DTM using poly space NPSPACE Decidable by NTM using poly space EXPTIME Decidable by DTM in \(2^{p(n)}\) time

docs.title: Basic Containments
docs.text:
Theorem

\[\mathbf{P} \subseteq \mathbf{PSPACE} \subseteq \mathbf{EXPTIME}\] Proof

P ⊆ PSPACE: Poly-time → uses at most poly tape cells.

PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME: With \(p(n)\) tape cells:

  • Number of configurations \(\leq |K| \cdot |\Sigma|^{p(n)} \cdot p(n) = 2^{O(p(n))}\)
  • Must halt within this many steps (no repeated configs)

docs.title: NP vs PSPACE
docs.text:
Theorem

\[\mathbf{NP} \subseteq \mathbf{PSPACE}\] Proof

Given NTM \(N\) deciding \(L\) in poly time:

  1. Simulate all branches of \(N\) sequentially
  2. Each branch uses poly space
  3. Track current branch with poly-space counter
  4. Accept if any branch accepts

docs.title: Savitch's Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Savitch)

\[\mathbf{NPSPACE} = \mathbf{PSPACE}\]

Key Insight

Non-determinism doesn't help for space (unlike time)!

Proof Idea

REACH problem: Can configuration \(C_1\) reach \(C_2\) in \(\leq t\) steps?

REACH(C₁, C₂, t):
  If t = 1:
    Return (C₁ = C₂) or (C₁ ⊢ C₂)
  Else:
    For each config C_m:
      If REACH(C₁, C_m, t/2) and REACH(C_m, C₂, t/2):
        Return TRUE
    Return FALSE

Space analysis:

  • Recursion depth: \(\log t = O(\log 2^{p(n)}) = O(p(n))\)
  • Each level stores one config: \(O(p(n))\) space
  • Total: \(O(p(n)^2)\) = polynomial!

docs.title: Space Hierarchy
docs.text:
Space Hierarchy Theorem

\[\mathbf{SPACE}(o(f(n))) \subsetneq \mathbf{SPACE}(f(n))\]

More space = strictly more problems solvable

Proof Sketch

Diagonalization construction:

Construct DTM \(D\) such that:

  1. \(D\) uses \(O(f(n))\) space
  2. \(D\) differs from every machine using \(o(f(n))\) space
D = On input ⟨M⟩x:
  1. Simulate M on ⟨M⟩x for f(n) space
  2. If M accepts within limit: REJECT
  3. If M rejects/exceeds: ACCEPT

     M₁  M₂  M₃  M₄  M₅  M₆  ...
M₁   +  
M₂   -   +
M₃   -   -   -
M₄   -   -   -   +
M₅   -   +   -   -   -
M₆   -   -   -   -   -   +
...
D    -   -   +   -   +   -   ...  (differs on diagonal)

docs.title: Time Hierarchy
docs.text:
Time Hierarchy Theorem

\[\mathbf{DTIME}(o(f(n))) \subsetneq \mathbf{DTIME}(f(n) \log f(n))\]

Note

Extra \(\log f(n)\) factor needed for counting steps!

docs.title: Complete Picture
docs.text:
Summary of Relationships

P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE = NPSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME
Containment Status P ⊆ NP Known (trivial) P ≠ EXPTIME Proven (hierarchy theorem) P = NP? Open NP = PSPACE? Open PSPACE = NPSPACE Proven (Savitch)

docs.title: Key Theorems Summary
docs.text:
What We Know

Theorem Statement Savitch NPSPACE = PSPACE Space Hierarchy More space = more power Time Hierarchy More time = more power P ≠ EXPTIME Follows from hierarchy

What We Don't Know

Question Status P = NP? Open (\(\$\)1 million prize) NP = PSPACE? Open P = PSPACE? Open

Philosophical Note

The hierarchy theorems tell us that more resources always help—there are problems requiring exactly \(n^{100}\) time that can't be solved in \(n^{99}\) time.

But whether a polynomial-time verifiable solution implies a polynomial-time algorithm remains one of the greatest open questions in mathematics!

docs.title: Regular Expressions
docs.text:
Overview

Regular expressions provide a declarative way to describe regular languages, complementing the operational description given by finite automata.

docs.title: Regular Expression Syntax
docs.text:
Example

\(a(a \cup b)^* b\) is a regular expression over \(\{a, b\}\)

\[L(R) = \{w \in \{a,b\}^* \mid w \text{ starts with } a \text{ and ends with } b\}\]

docs.title: Atomic Regular Expressions
docs.text: Expression Language \(\emptyset\) \(L(\emptyset) = \emptyset\) (empty language) \(a \in \Sigma\) \(L(a) = \{a\}\) (single symbol)

docs.title: Composition Rules
docs.text:
Building Complex Expressions

Operation Notation Language Union \(R_1 \cup R_2\) \(L(R_1 \cup R_2) = L(R_1) \cup L(R_2)\) Concatenation \(R_1 R_2\) \(L(R_1 R_2) = L(R_1) L(R_2)\) Kleene Star \(R_1^*\) \(L(R_1^*) = [L(R_1)]^*\)

docs.title: Operator Precedence
docs.text:
Precedence (highest to lowest)

\[\text{Kleene Star } (*) \quad > \quad \text{Concatenation } (\cdot) \quad > \quad \text{Union } (\cup)\]

docs.title: Theorem 1: RE → NFA
docs.text:
Theorem

Every regular expression can be converted to an equivalent NFA.

The construction follows the recursive structure of the regular expression.

docs.title: Theorem 1: NFA → RE (State Elimination)
docs.text:
Theorem

Every NFA can be converted to an equivalent regular expression using state elimination.

State Elimination Method

Idea: Use dynamic programming to eliminate states one by one, updating transition labels with regular expressions.

docs.title: The Pumping Lemma
docs.text:
Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages

Let \(L\) be a regular language. There exists an integer \(p \geq 1\) (called the pumping length) such that:

Every string \(w \in L\) with \(|w| \geq p\) can be written as \(w = xyz\) satisfying:

  1. \(|xy| \leq p\)
  2. \(|y| \geq 1\)
  3. For all \(i \geq 0\): \(xy^i z \in L\)
Proof Sketch

Case 1: Finite \(L\)

Set \(p = \max\{|w| : w \in L\} + 1\). No string in \(L\) has length \(\geq p\), so the lemma holds vacuously.

Case 2: Infinite \(L\)

Let NFA \(N\) with \(n\) states accept \(L\). Set \(p = n + 1\).

For any \(w \in L\) with \(|w| \geq p\):

  • Consider the sequence of states \(q_0, q_1, \ldots, q_{|w|}\) visited while reading \(w\)
  • By pigeonhole principle: \(\exists i \neq j\) with \(q_i = q_j\) (within first \(p\) states)
  • Set: \(x = w[0..i-1]\), \(y = w[i..j-1]\), \(z = w[j..|w|-1]\)
  • The loop from \(q_i\) back to \(q_i = q_j\) can be pumped!

docs.title: Applications: Proving Non-Regularity
docs.text:
Strategy

To prove \(L\) is not regular:

  1. Assume \(L\) is regular (for contradiction)
  2. Let \(p\) be the pumping length
  3. Choose a clever string \(w \in L\) with \(|w| \geq p\)
  4. Show that no valid decomposition \(w = xyz\) satisfies all three conditions

docs.title: Example 1: \(\{0^n 1^n \mid n \geq 0\}\)
docs.text:
Proof

Claim: \(L = \{0^n 1^n \mid n \geq 0\}\) is not regular.

Proof by contradiction:

  1. Assume \(L\) is regular with pumping length \(p\)
  2. Consider \(w = 0^p 1^p \in L\) (clearly \(|w| = 2p \geq p\))
  3. By pumping lemma, \(w = xyz\) with \(|xy| \leq p\) and \(|y| \geq 1\)
  4. Since \(|xy| \leq p\), we have \(y = 0^k\) for some \(k \geq 1\)
  5. Then \(xy^2z = 0^{p+k} 1^p \notin L\) ❌

Contradiction! Therefore \(L\) is not regular. ∎

docs.title: Example 2: Equal 0s and 1s
docs.text:
Proof using Closure Properties

Claim: \(L = \{w \in \{0,1\}^* \mid w \text{ has equal 0s and 1s}\}\) is not regular.

Proof:

  1. Assume \(L\) is regular
  2. \(0^* 1^*\) is regular (easy to construct FA)
  3. By closure under intersection: \(L \cap 0^* 1^* = \{0^n 1^n \mid n \geq 0\}\) would be regular
  4. But we proved \(\{0^n 1^n\}\) is not regular! ❌

Contradiction! ∎

Summary

Topic Key Point Regular Expressions Declarative description of regular languages RE ↔ NFA Equivalent expressive power Pumping Lemma Tool for proving non-regularity Proof Strategy Contradiction + clever string choice

docs.title: Context-Free Grammars
docs.text:
Overview

Context-Free Grammars (CFGs) are more powerful than regular expressions, capable of describing nested structures like balanced parentheses and programming language syntax.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Context-Free Grammar

A CFG \(G = (V, \Sigma, R, S)\) consists of:

Component Description \(V\) Finite set of variables (non-terminals) \(\Sigma\) Finite set of terminal symbols \(S \in V - \Sigma\) Start symbol \(R \subseteq (V - \Sigma) \times V^*\) Finite set of production rules

docs.title: Derivation
docs.text:
One-Step Derivation (\(\Rightarrow\))

For any \(x, y, u \in V^*\) and \(A \in V - \Sigma\):

\[xAy \Rightarrow xuy \quad \text{if } (A, u) \in R\]

Multi-Step Derivation (\(\Rightarrow^*\))

\[w \Rightarrow^* u \quad \text{if } w = u \text{ or } w \Rightarrow u_1 \Rightarrow u_2 \Rightarrow \cdots \Rightarrow u\]

docs.title: Language of a Grammar
docs.text:
Definition

\(G\) generates \(w \in \Sigma^*\) if \(S \Rightarrow^* w\)

\[L(G) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid G \text{ generates } w\}\]

Such a language is called a Context-Free Language (CFL).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Example 1: \(\{a^n b^n \mid n \geq 0\}\)

Grammar: 

S → aSb | ε

Derivation of \(aabb\): \(\(S \Rightarrow aSb \Rightarrow aaSbb \Rightarrow aabb\)\)

Example 2: Palindromes \(\{w \in \{a,b\}^* \mid w = w^R\}\)

Grammar: 

S → aSa | bSb | a | b | ε

Derivation of \(abba\): \(\(S \Rightarrow aSa \Rightarrow abSba \Rightarrow abba\)\)

docs.title: Leftmost Derivation
docs.text:
Definition

A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost variable first.

Ambiguity

A grammar is ambiguous if some string has multiple leftmost derivations (or equivalently, multiple parse trees).

docs.title: Pumping Lemma for CFLs
docs.text:
Pumping Lemma for Context-Free Languages

If \(L\) is a context-free language, there exists \(p \geq 1\) such that:

Every \(s \in L\) with \(|s| \geq p\) can be written as \(s = uvxyz\) satisfying:

  1. \(|vxy| \leq p\)
  2. \(|vy| \geq 1\) (at least one of \(v, y\) is non-empty)
  3. For all \(i \geq 0\): \(uv^i xy^i z \in L\)

Key Difference from Regular Pumping Lemma

  • Regular: pump one substring (\(y\))
  • Context-Free: pump two substrings simultaneously (\(v\) and \(y\))
Proof Intuition

In a sufficiently long derivation tree:

  • Some variable must repeat on a root-to-leaf path
  • The subtree rooted at this repeated variable can be "pumped"

See detailed proofs:

  • Lawrence University Notes
  • UIUC CS 373

docs.title: Example: \(\{a^n b^n c^n \mid n \geq 0\}\)
docs.text:
Theorem

\(L = \{a^n b^n c^n \mid n \geq 0\}\) is not context-free.

Proof

By contradiction:

  1. Assume \(L\) is context-free with pumping length \(p\)
  2. Consider \(s = a^p b^p c^p \in L\)
  3. By pumping lemma: \(s = uvxyz\) with \(|vxy| \leq p\) and \(|vy| \geq 1\)

Key observation: Since \(|vxy| \leq p\), the substring \(vxy\) can contain at most two different symbols from \(\{a, b, c\}\).

Case analysis:

Case \(vxy\) contains Pumping \(uv^2xy^2z\) 1 only \(a\)'s Too many \(a\)'s 2 only \(b\)'s Too many \(b\)'s 3 only \(c\)'s Too many \(c\)'s 4 \(a\)'s and \(b\)'s Wrong count of \(c\)'s 5 \(b\)'s and \(c\)'s Wrong count of \(a\)'s

In all cases, \(uv^2xy^2z \notin L\) ❌

Contradiction! ∎

docs.title: Hierarchy Summary
docs.text:
Chomsky Hierarchy (so far)

Regular Languages ⊂ Context-Free Languages ⊂ ???
Class Recognizer Generator Regular DFA / NFA Regular Expression Context-Free PDA (next lecture) CFG

Key Takeaways

Concept Description CFG 4-tuple \((V, \Sigma, R, S)\) with production rules CFL Language generated by some CFG Derivation Sequence of rule applications Parse Tree Tree representation of derivation Pumping Lemma Tool to prove non-context-freeness Limitation \(\{a^n b^n c^n\}\) is not context-free

docs.title: Pushdown Automata
docs.text:
Overview

Pushdown Automata (PDA) extend finite automata with a stack, enabling them to recognize context-free languages. The stack provides "memory" for matching nested structures.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Pushdown Automaton

A PDA is a 6-tuple \(P = (K, \Sigma, \Gamma, \Delta, s, F)\):

Component Description \(K\) Finite set of states \(\Sigma\) Tape alphabet (input symbols) \(\Gamma\) Stack alphabet \(\Delta\) Set of transition rules \(s \in K\) Initial state \(F \subseteq K\) Set of accepting states

docs.title: Transition Rules
docs.text:
Transition Relation \(\Delta\)

\[\Delta \subseteq K \times (\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}) \times \Gamma^* \times K \times \Gamma^*\]

A transition \(((q, a, \gamma), (p, \beta)) \in \Delta\) means:

From Read Pop To Push State \(q\) Symbol \(a\) \(\gamma\) from stack State \(p\) \(\beta\) onto stack

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Definition

A configuration of a PDA is a triple \((q, x, \alpha) \in K \times \Sigma^* \times \Gamma^*\):

  • \(q\) — current state
  • \(x\) — remaining input
  • \(\alpha\) — current stack contents (top on left)

docs.title: Yield Relations
docs.text:
One-Step Yield (\(\vdash_P\))

\((q, x, \alpha) \vdash_P (p, y, \beta)\) if there exists \(((q, a, r), (p, b)) \in \Delta\) such that:

  • \(x = ay\) (read symbol \(a\))
  • \(\alpha = r\tau\) (pop \(r\) from stack)
  • \(\beta = b\tau\) (push \(b\) onto stack)

Multi-Step Yield (\(\vdash_P^*\))

\((q, x, \alpha) \vdash_P^* (p, y, \beta)\) if reachable in zero or more steps.

docs.title: Language Acceptance
docs.text:
Language of PDA

PDA \(P\) accepts string \(x\) if: \(\((s, x, \varepsilon) \vdash_P^* (f, \varepsilon, \varepsilon) \quad \text{for some } f \in F\)\)

\[L(P) = \{x \in \Sigma^* \mid P \text{ accepts } x\}\]

docs.title: Example: Equal 0s and 1s
docs.text:
Language: \(\{w \in \{0,1\}^* \mid \#0\text{'s} = \#1\text{'s}\}\)

PDA Components:

Component Value \(K\) \(\{s, q, f\}\) \(\Sigma\) \(\{0, 1\}\) \(\Gamma\) \(\{\$, 0, 1\}\) Start \(s\) Accept \(\{f\}\) Transition Rules Current Input Stack Top Next Stack Action \(s\) \(\varepsilon\) \(\varepsilon\) \(q\) push \(\$\) \(q\) \(0\) \(\$\) \(q\) push \(0\$\) \(q\) \(0\) \(0\) \(q\) push \(00\) \(q\) \(0\) \(1\) \(q\) pop (cancel) \(q\) \(1\) \(\$\) \(q\) push \(1\$\) \(q\) \(1\) \(0\) \(q\) pop (cancel) \(q\) \(1\) \(1\) \(q\) push \(11\) \(q\) \(\varepsilon\) \(\$\) \(f\) pop \(\$\)

docs.title: CFG ↔ PDA Equivalence
docs.text:
Theorem

CFG ⇔ PDA: A language is context-free if and only if it is accepted by some PDA.

docs.title: CFG → PDA Construction
docs.text:
Example: \(S \rightarrow aSb \mid \varepsilon\)

PDA Construction:

  • \(K = \{s, f\}\)
  • \(\Gamma = V\) (all grammar symbols)

Transitions:

Type Rule Initialize \((s, \varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to (f, S)\) — push start symbol Generate \((f, \varepsilon, A) \to (f, u)\) for each rule \(A \to u\) Match \((f, a, a) \to (f, \varepsilon)\) for each terminal \(a\)

docs.title: PDA → CFG Construction
docs.text:
Method

  1. Convert PDA to Simple PDA (single push/pop per transition)
  2. Convert Simple PDA to CFG using variable naming scheme

docs.title: Theorem: Regular ⊂ Context-Free
docs.text:
Theorem

Every regular language is context-free.

Proof Methods
  • NFA → PDA: Add stack that's never used
  • DFA → CFG: Create rules mimicking transitions

docs.title: Closure Properties of CFLs
docs.text:
CFLs are closed under:

Operation Construction Union Add rule \(S \to S_1 \mid S_2\) Concatenation Add rule \(S \to S_1 S_2\) Kleene Star Add rule \(S \to SS_A \mid \varepsilon\)

CFLs are NOT closed under:

  • Intersection (\(\cap\))
  • Complement (\(\overline{L}\))
Proof: Not Closed under Intersection

Consider:

  • \(A = \{a^i b^j c^k \mid i = j\}\) — CFL ✓
  • \(B = \{a^i b^j c^k \mid j = k\}\) — CFL ✓
  • \(A \cap B = \{a^n b^n c^n \mid n \geq 0\}\) — NOT CFL! ❌

Since \(\overline{A \cap B} = \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}\), closure under complement would imply closure under intersection.

docs.title: Advanced Example
docs.text:
Language: \(\{w \in \{a,b\}^* \mid \#a = 2 \cdot \#b\}\)

Idea: Use stack as a unary counter with \(+\) and \(-\) symbols.

Component Value \(K\) \(\{s\}\) \(\Sigma\) \(\{a, b\}\) \(\Gamma\) \(\{+, -\}\) Start/Accept \(s\) Transitions Input Stack Action Meaning \(b\) \(\varepsilon\) push \(++\) Need 2 more \(a\)'s \(b\) \(-\) replace with \(+\) Cancel one, need one more \(b\) \(--\) pop both Balanced \(a\) \(\varepsilon\) push \(-\) Owe one \(b\) (half) \(a\) \(+\) pop Cancel debt

Summary

Concept Key Point PDA NFA + Stack Power Recognizes exactly CFLs CFG ↔ PDA Equivalent models Closure ∪, ·, * but NOT ∩, complement Stack Usage Can simulate counters

docs.title: Turing Machine
docs.text:
Overview

The Turing Machine, invented by Alan Turing in 1936, is the most powerful model of computation. It can simulate any computer algorithm and forms the theoretical foundation of modern computing.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Turing Machine

A Turing Machine is a 5-tuple \((K, \Sigma, \delta, s, H)\):

Component Description \(K\) Finite set of states \(\Sigma\) Finite set of tape symbols (includes \(\triangleright\) and \(\sqcup\)) \(s \in K\) Start state \(H \subseteq K\) Halt states (typically \(\{yes, no\}\)) \(\delta\) Transition function

docs.title: Transition Function
docs.text:
\[\delta: (K - H) \times \Sigma \rightarrow K \times (\Sigma \cup \{L, R\})\]

Special Symbols

  • \(\triangleright\) — Left endmarker (cannot be overwritten)
  • \(\sqcup\) — Blank symbol (infinite supply on tape)

Constraints:

  • \(\forall q \in K - H\): \(\delta(q, \triangleright) = (p, R)\) for some \(p\) (must move right from endmarker)
  • Actions: write a symbol OR move (\(L\)/\(R\))

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Definition

A configuration is a snapshot of the TM's state: \(\((q, \triangleright w \underline{a} u) \in K \times \triangleright \Sigma^*\)\)

  • \(q\) — current state
  • \(w\) — tape contents to the left of head
  • \(a\) — symbol under head (underlined)
  • \(u\) — tape contents to the right

docs.title: Yield Relations
docs.text:
Notation Meaning \((q_1, \triangleright w_1 a_1 u_1) \vdash_M (q_2, \triangleright w_2 a_2 u_2)\) One-step transition \(\vdash_M^*\) Zero or more steps

Transition types:

  • Write: \(\delta(q_1, a_1) = (q_2, a_2)\) where \(a_2 \in \Sigma\)
  • Move Left: \(\delta(q_1, a_1) = (q_2, L)\)
  • Move Right: \(\delta(q_1, a_1) = (q_2, R)\)

docs.title: Acceptance
docs.text:
Definitions

Term Meaning \(M\) accepts \(w\) \((s, \triangleright \sqcup w) \vdash^* (yes, \ldots)\) \(M\) rejects \(w\) \((s, \triangleright \sqcup w) \vdash^* (no, \ldots)\) \(L(M)\) \(\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid M \text{ accepts } w\}\)

docs.title: Decidability
docs.text:
Key Definitions

Term Definition \(M\) decides \(L\) \(M\) accepts all \(w \in L\) AND rejects all \(w \notin L\) \(M\) semi-decides \(L\) \(M\) accepts all \(w \in L\) (may loop on \(w \notin L\)) Recursive language Decided by some TM Recursively Enumerable Semi-decided by some TM

Important

Every recursive language is recursively enumerable, but not vice versa!

docs.title: Multi-tape TM
docs.text: \[\delta: (K - H) \times \Sigma^k \rightarrow K \times ((\Sigma - \{\triangleright\}) \cup \{L, R\})^k\]

docs.title: Other Variants
docs.text:
Variant Description Two-way infinite tape No left endmarker Multi-head TM Multiple heads on one tape 2D-tape TM Two-dimensional tape Random Access TM Can jump to any position

Equivalence Theorem

All variants are equivalent in computational power to the standard TM!

docs.title: Example: \(\{a^n b^n c^n\}\)
docs.text:
TM for \(L = \{a^n b^n c^n \mid n \geq 0\}\)

High-level algorithm:

  1. Check format: only \(a\)'s, then \(b\)'s, then \(c\)'s
  2. Mark leftmost \(a\) with \(X\)
  3. Scan right, mark leftmost \(b\) with \(Y\)
  4. Scan right, mark leftmost \(c\) with \(Z\)
  5. Return to leftmost unmarked \(a\), repeat
  6. Accept if all symbols are marked

docs.title: Non-deterministic TM
docs.text:
Definition

NTM uses a transition relation instead of function: \(\(\Delta \subseteq (K - H) \times \Sigma \times K \times (\Sigma \cup \{L, R\})\)\)

docs.title: Acceptance (NTM)
docs.text:
NTM Semantics

  • Accepts \(w\): Some computation path reaches \(yes\)
  • Rejects \(w\): All computation paths reach \(no\)
  • Decides \(L\): All branches halt; accepts iff \(w \in L\)
  • Semi-decides \(L\): Accepts iff \(w \in L\); may not halt

docs.title: Example: Composite Numbers
docs.text:
NTM for \(C = \{n \in \mathbb{N} \mid n \text{ is composite}\}\)

NTM = On input n:
  1. Non-deterministically guess factors a, b > 1
  2. Verify a × b = n
  3. If yes, ACCEPT

docs.title: NTM = DTM Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem

Every NTM can be simulated by a DTM.

Proof: BFS Simulation

Use a 3-tape DTM:

  1. Tape 1: Input
  2. Tape 2: Working tape for simulation
  3. Tape 3: BFS queue of configurations

docs.title: Church-Turing Thesis
docs.text:
Church-Turing Thesis

Every algorithm can be simulated by a Turing Machine.

Intuitive notion of "computability" = Turing computability

docs.title: Encoding Facts
docs.text:
What Can Be Encoded

  • Any finite set can be encoded as a string
  • Any finite tuple of finite sets can be encoded
  • Graphs \(G = (V, E)\) can be encoded

docs.title: \(A_{DFA}\): DFA Acceptance
docs.text:
\(A_{DFA} = \{\langle D, w \rangle \mid D \text{ accepts } w\}\)

M = On input ⟨D, w⟩:
  1. Simulate D on w
  2. Accept if D accepts; Reject otherwise

✓ Decidable

docs.title: \(A_{NFA}\): NFA Acceptance
docs.text:
\(A_{NFA} = \{\langle B, w \rangle \mid B \text{ accepts } w\}\)

Reduction: NFA → DFA → solve \(A_{DFA}\)

✓ Decidable

docs.title: \(E_{DFA}\): DFA Emptiness
docs.text:
\(E_{DFA} = \{\langle D \rangle \mid L(D) = \emptyset\}\)

M = On input ⟨D⟩:
  1. DFS from start state
  2. ACCEPT if no accepting state reachable
  3. REJECT otherwise

✓ Decidable

docs.title: \(EQ_{DFA}\): DFA Equivalence
docs.text:
\(EQ_{DFA} = \{\langle D_1, D_2 \rangle \mid L(D_1) = L(D_2)\}\)

Idea: Check if symmetric difference is empty \(\(L(D_1) \triangle L(D_2) = (L(D_1) \cup L(D_2)) - (L(D_1) \cap L(D_2))\)\)

✓ Decidable

docs.title: \(A_{CFG}\): CFG Membership
docs.text:
\(A_{CFG} = \{\langle G, w \rangle \mid G \text{ generates } w\}\)

Using Chomsky Normal Form:

  • Convert \(G\) to CNF
  • Enumerate all derivations of length \(\leq 2|w| - 1\)

✓ Decidable (CYK algorithm: \(O(n^3)\))

Summary Table

Problem Input Decidable? \(A_{DFA}\) DFA + string ✓ \(A_{NFA}\) NFA + string ✓ \(A_{REX}\) Regex + string ✓ \(E_{DFA}\) DFA ✓ \(EQ_{DFA}\) Two DFAs ✓ \(A_{CFG}\) CFG + string ✓ \(A_{PDA}\) PDA + string ✓ \(E_{CFG}\) CFG ✓

docs.title: Language Containment Properties
docs.text:
Overview

This lecture establishes the Chomsky Hierarchy of language classes and proves fundamental results about decidability using counting arguments and diagonalization.

docs.title: The Chomsky Hierarchy
docs.text:
Language Containment

\[\text{Regular} \subsetneq \text{Context-Free} \subsetneq \text{Recursive} \subsetneq \text{Recursively Enumerable}\] Separation Example Language Regular → CF \(\{a^n b^n \mid n \geq 0\}\) CF → Recursive \(\{a^n b^n c^n \mid n \geq 0\}\) Recursive → RE \(A_{TM}\) (halting problem)

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
Countable Set

A set \(A\) is countable if:

  • \(A\) is finite, OR
  • There exists a bijection \(f: A \to \mathbb{N}\)

docs.title: Key Lemmas
docs.text:
Lemma 1: Injection Characterization

\(A\) is countable \(\iff\) there exists an injection \(f: A \to \mathbb{N}\)

Proof

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Bijection implies injection (trivial).

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Given injection \(f: A \to \mathbb{N}\):

  1. Sort elements of \(A\) by their \(f\)-values
  2. Define bijection \(g: A \to \mathbb{N}\) by position in sorted order

Corollary 1

Any subset of a countable set is countable.

docs.title: Countability Results
docs.text:
Lemma 2: \(\Sigma^*\) is Countable

For any finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), the set of all strings \(\Sigma^*\) is countable.

Proof Sketch

Enumerate strings by: 1. First by length 2. Then lexicographically within each length

See Waterloo Notes, Proposition 2.1

Corollary 2

The set of all Turing Machines is countable.

Proof: Each TM has a finite description, encodable as a string.

docs.title: Uncountability
docs.text:
Lemma 3: Languages are Uncountable

The set of all languages over alphabet \(\Sigma\) is uncountable.

Proof (Cantor's Diagonal Argument)

Assume languages are countable: \(L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots\)

Construct \(L^* = \{w_i \mid w_i \notin L_i\}\)

Then \(L^* \neq L_i\) for all \(i\) — contradiction!

Fundamental Theorem

Since:

  • Turing Machines are countable
  • Languages are uncountable

There exist languages that are NOT recursively enumerable!

docs.title: \(A_{TM}\): The Acceptance Problem
docs.text:
Definition

\[A_{TM} = \{\langle M, w \rangle \mid M \text{ is a TM and } M \text{ accepts } w\}\]

docs.title: Theorem 1: \(A_{TM}\) is RE
docs.text:
Theorem

\(A_{TM}\) is recursively enumerable (semi-decidable).

Proof

Construct TM \(E\) that semi-decides \(A_{TM}\):

E = On input ⟨M, w⟩:
  1. Simulate M on w
  2. If M accepts → ACCEPT
  3. If M rejects → REJECT
  4. If M loops → LOOP (never halt)

docs.title: Theorem 2: \(A_{TM}\) is NOT Recursive
docs.text:
Theorem

\(A_{TM}\) is not recursive (undecidable).

Proof (Diagonalization)

Assume \(A_{TM}\) is recursive. Then some TM \(H\) decides it.

Construct TM \(D\): 

D = On input ⟨M⟩:
  1. Run H on ⟨M, ⟨M⟩⟩
  2. If H accepts → REJECT
  3. If H rejects → ACCEPT

Paradox: What happens when \(D\) runs on \(\langle D \rangle\)?

If \(D\) on \(\langle D \rangle\)... Then \(H\) on \(\langle D, \langle D \rangle \rangle\)... Contradiction! accepts accepts (so \(D\) rejects) ❌ rejects rejects (so \(D\) accepts) ❌

Therefore, \(H\) cannot exist, and \(A_{TM}\) is undecidable. ∎

docs.title: \(A_d\): Diagonal Non-Acceptance
docs.text:
Definition

\[A_d = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ is a TM that does NOT accept } \langle M \rangle\}\]

docs.title: Theorem 3: \(A_d\) is NOT RE
docs.text:
Theorem

\(A_d\) is not recursively enumerable.

Proof

Assume TM \(D\) semi-decides \(A_d\): 

D = On input ⟨M⟩:
  1. If M ∈ A_d (M rejects ⟨M⟩) → ACCEPT
  2. If M ∉ A_d (M accepts ⟨M⟩) → REJECT or LOOP

Paradox: Run \(D\) on \(\langle D \rangle\):

If \(D\) on \(\langle D \rangle\)... Then... Contradiction! accepts \(D \in A_d\) means \(D\) rejects \(\langle D \rangle\) ❌ rejects/loops \(D \notin A_d\) means \(D\) accepts \(\langle D \rangle\) ❌

docs.title: Theorem 4: RE + co-RE = Recursive
docs.text:
Theorem

If both \(L\) and \(\overline{L}\) are RE, then \(L\) is recursive.

Proof

Let \(M_1\) semi-decide \(L\) and \(M_2\) semi-decide \(\overline{L}\).

Construct decider \(D\): 

D = On input w:
  1. Run M₁ and M₂ in parallel on w
  2. If M₁ accepts → ACCEPT
  3. If M₂ accepts → REJECT

One of them must accept (since \(w \in L\) or \(w \in \overline{L}\)).

docs.title: Theorem 5: \(\overline{A_{TM}}\) is NOT RE
docs.text:
Theorem

\(\overline{A_{TM}}\) is not recursively enumerable.

Proof
  • We know \(A_{TM}\) is RE
  • We know \(A_{TM}\) is NOT recursive
  • By Theorem 4: If \(\overline{A_{TM}}\) were RE, then \(A_{TM}\) would be recursive
  • Contradiction! ∎

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text:
Classification of Key Languages

Language Recursive? RE? co-RE? Regular languages ✓ ✓ ✓ CFLs ✓ ✓ ✓ \(A_{TM}\) ❌ ✓ ❌ \(\overline{A_{TM}}\) ❌ ❌ ✓ \(A_d\) ❌ ❌ ?

Key Insight

The diagonal argument is the fundamental technique for proving undecidability. It creates a paradox by self-reference.

docs.title: Undecidable Problems
docs.text:
Overview

This lecture explores problems that cannot be solved by any algorithm, using reduction techniques to prove undecidability.

docs.title: Proof 2: Reduction from \(A_{TM}\)
docs.text:
Theorem

\(H_{TM} = \{\langle M, w \rangle \mid M \text{ halts on } w\}\) is undecidable.

Proof

Assume \(H_{TM}\) is decidable by TM \(M_H\).

Construct \(M^*\) to solve \(A_{TM}\): 

M* = On input ⟨M, w⟩:
  1. Run M_H on ⟨M, w⟩
  2. If M_H rejects (M doesn't halt) → REJECT
  3. Else simulate M on w:
     - If M accepts → ACCEPT
     - If M rejects → REJECT

But \(A_{TM}\) is undecidable! Contradiction. ∎

docs.title: Problem 1: Accept Empty String
docs.text:
\(L_1 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } \varepsilon\}\)

Undecidable!

Proof: Reduction from \(A_{TM}\)

Given \(\langle M, w \rangle\), construct \(M^*\): 

M* = On input x:
  1. Ignore x
  2. Run M on w
  3. If M accepts → ACCEPT
  4. If M rejects → REJECT

\(M\) on \(w\) \(M^*\) behavior \(M^* \in L_1\)? Accepts Accepts everything (including \(\varepsilon\)) Yes Rejects/Loops Rejects/loops on everything No

So: \(\langle M, w \rangle \in A_{TM} \iff \langle M^* \rangle \in L_1\)

docs.title: Problem 2: Accept All Strings
docs.text:
\(L_2 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid L(M) = \Sigma^*\}\)

Undecidable! (Same reduction idea)

docs.title: Problem 3: Language Equivalence
docs.text:
\(L_3 = \{\langle M_1, M_2 \rangle \mid L(M_1) = L(M_2)\}\)

Undecidable!

Proof: Reduction from \(L_2\)

Construct \(M_E\) that accepts everything: 

M_E = On input x:
  1. ACCEPT

Then: \(\langle M \rangle \in L_2 \iff \langle M, M_E \rangle \in L_3\)

docs.title: Problem 4: Is Language Regular?
docs.text:
\(L_4 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid L(M) \text{ is regular}\}\)

Undecidable!

Proof

Given \(\langle M, w \rangle\), construct \(M^*\): 

M* = On input x:
  1. Run M on w
  2. If M accepts w:
     - Simulate Universal TM U on x
     - Accept iff U accepts
  3. If M doesn't accept w:
     - REJECT (or never reach here)

\(M\) on \(w\) \(L(M^*)\) Regular? Accepts \(A_{TM}\) (not regular!) No Doesn't accept \(\emptyset\) Yes

Corollary

Similarly undecidable:

  • \(L_5 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid L(M) \text{ is context-free}\}\)
  • \(L_6 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid L(M) \text{ is recursive}\}\)

docs.title: Rice's Theorem
docs.text:
Rice's Theorem

Any non-trivial property of the language recognized by a TM is undecidable.

Non-trivial = some TMs have it, some don't

See UIUC Lecture Notes

docs.title: \(All_{PDA}\) is Undecidable
docs.text:
Theorem

\(All_{PDA} = \{\langle P \rangle \mid L(P) = \Sigma^*\}\) is undecidable.

Proof Sketch

Key idea: Encode TM computation histories as strings.

A computation history of \(M\) on \(w\): \(\(C_1 \# C_2 \# \ldots \# C_k\)\)

where \(C_i\) are configurations.

Construct PDA \(P\) that accepts strings that are NOT valid accepting computation histories:

Accept if:

  1. \(C_1\) is not the start configuration, OR
  2. \(C_k\) is not an accepting configuration, OR
  3. Some \(C_i \not\vdash C_{i+1}\)

Then: \(L(P) = \Sigma^* \iff M\) doesn't halt on \(w\)

This reduces \(H_{TM}\) to \(\overline{All_{PDA}}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Many-One Reduction

Language \(A\) reduces to \(B\) (written \(A \leq_m B\)) if there exists computable \(f: \Sigma^* \to \Sigma^*\) such that: \(\(x \in A \iff f(x) \in B\)\)

docs.title: Key Lemmas
docs.text:
Lemma 1

If \(A \leq_m B\) and \(B\) is recursive, then \(A\) is recursive.

Proof 
M_A = On input x:
  1. Compute f(x)
  2. Run M_B on f(x)
  3. Accept iff M_B accepts

Lemma 2 (Contrapositive)

If \(A\) is not recursive and \(A \leq_m B\), then \(B\) is not recursive.

docs.title: Summary of Reductions
docs.text:
graph TD
    ATM[A_TM undecidable] --> HTM[H_TM]
    ATM --> L1[Accept ε]
    ATM --> L2[Accept Σ*]
    L2 --> L3[Language Equality]
    ATM --> L4[Is Regular?]
    HTM --> AllPDA[All_PDA]

Reduction Strategy

To prove \(L\) undecidable:

  1. Choose known undecidable problem \(A\) (usually \(A_{TM}\) or \(H_{TM}\))
  2. Show \(A \leq_m L\) by constructing computable \(f\)
  3. Conclude \(L\) is undecidable

Common Undecidable Problems

Problem Description \(A_{TM}\) Does \(M\) accept \(w\)? \(H_{TM}\) Does \(M\) halt on \(w\)? \(E_{TM}\) Is \(L(M) = \emptyset\)? \(EQ_{TM}\) Is \(L(M_1) = L(M_2)\)? \(REG_{TM}\) Is \(L(M)\) regular? \(All_{PDA}\) Is \(L(P) = \Sigma^*\)?

docs.title: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems
docs.text:
Overview

This lecture explores self-reference in computation, the Recursion Theorem, and Gödel's profound results about the limits of formal systems.

docs.title: Quines: Self-Printing Programs
docs.text:
Goal

Construct a TM \(M\) that prints its own description \(\langle M \rangle\).

Construction using two parts:

A = On any input:
    1. Write "B" on the tape

B = On input w:
    1. Compute q(w)  // q(w) = ⟨M_w⟩ where M_w prints w
    2. Write q(w) and swap with w

Helper Function \(q\)

\(q: \Sigma^* \to \Sigma^*\) where \(q(w) = \langle M_w \rangle\)

\(M_w\) = On any input: print \(w\)

docs.title: The Recursion Theorem
docs.text:
Recursion Theorem

For any TM \(T\), there exists a TM \(R\) such that for any input \(w\):

\[\text{Computation of } R \text{ on } w = \text{Computation of } T \text{ on } \langle R, w \rangle\]

In other words: \(R\) can "know" its own description!

T = On input ⟨M, w⟩:
    ... (uses M's description)

R = On input w:
    1. Obtain own description "R"
    2. Run T on ⟨R, w⟩

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Proof System

A proof system for language \(\tau\) is a TM \(V\) satisfying:

Property Meaning Effectiveness \(V(x, y)\) always halts Soundness If \(x \notin \tau\), then \(\forall y: V(x, y) = 0\)

\(V\) is complete if: \(\forall x \in \tau, \exists y: V(x, y) = 1\)

docs.title: Theorem 1: Incomplete Proof Systems Exist
docs.text:
Theorem

Some languages have no complete proof system.

docs.title: Lemma: RE ↔ Complete Proof System
docs.text:
Lemma

\(A\) has a complete proof system \(\iff\) \(A\) is recursively enumerable.

Proof

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Given complete proof system \(V\): 

M = On input x:
  For y in Σ* (increasing length):
    If V(x, y) = 1: ACCEPT
\(M\) semi-decides \(A\).

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Given TM \(M\) that semi-decides \(A\): 

V = On input (x, y):
  Run M on x for |y| steps
  If M accepts within |y| steps: ACCEPT
  Else: REJECT

docs.title: Theorem 2: \(\overline{A_{TM}}\) Has No Complete Proof System
docs.text:
Theorem

\(\overline{A_{TM}}\) is not recursively enumerable.

Equivalently: No complete proof system exists for "\(M\) doesn't accept \(w\)".

Proof (Using Recursion Theorem)

Assume \(V\) is a complete proof system for \(\overline{A_{TM}}\).

Construct: 

R = On input x:
  1. Obtain own description "R"
  2. For y in Σ* (increasing length):
     If V(⟨R⟩x, y) = 1: HALT and ACCEPT

Paradox:

  • If \(R\) accepts \(x\): Then \(\langle R, x \rangle \notin \overline{A_{TM}}\), so \(V\) shouldn't accept
  • If \(R\) doesn't accept: Then \(\langle R, x \rangle \in \overline{A_{TM}}\), so \(V\) should accept, making \(R\) accept

Contradiction! ∎

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Turing Enumerator

TM \(M\) enumerates language \(L\) if there's an output state \(q\) such that: \(\(L = \{w \mid (s, \triangleright \sqcup) \vdash^*_M (q, \ldots w)\}\)\)

docs.title: Theorem 3: Enumerable = RE
docs.text:
Theorem

\(A\) is Turing enumerable \(\iff\) \(A\) is recursively enumerable.

Proof

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Trivial by definition.

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Given TM \(M\) that semi-decides \(A\): 

Enumerator E:
  For i = 1, 2, 3, ...:
    For j = 1, 2, ..., i:
      Run M on s_j for i steps
      If M accepts: OUTPUT s_j

This "dovetailing" ensures every accepted string is eventually output.

docs.title: Theorem 4
docs.text:
Definition

TM \(M\) is minimal if no smaller TM recognizes \(L(M)\): \(\(|N| < |M| \implies L(N) \neq L(M)\)\)

docs.title: Summary: Gödel's Results
docs.text:
Philosophical Implications

First Incompleteness Theorem: Any consistent formal system capable of expressing arithmetic contains statements that are true but unprovable within the system.

Second Incompleteness Theorem: Such a system cannot prove its own consistency.

Statement Formalization "This statement is unprovable" Encoded as formula in arithmetic True but unprovable Corresponds to \(\langle M, w \rangle \in \overline{A_{TM}}\) with no proof Consistency unprovable Related to halting problem

Key Takeaways

Concept Result Recursion Theorem TMs can access their own description RE = Complete Proof Language is RE iff provable \(\overline{A_{TM}}\) No complete proof system Gödel Limits of formal reasoning

docs.title: Time Complexity
docs.text:
Overview

This lecture introduces complexity theory, studying the computational resources (time, space) required to solve problems. We define the classes P and NP and explore NP-completeness.

docs.title: Running Time
docs.text:
Definition

For a DTM \(M\) that halts on all inputs, the running time is: \(\(f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\)\) where \(f(n)\) = max steps on any input of length \(n\).

docs.title: Time Complexity Classes
docs.text:
DTIME

\[\text{DTIME}(t(n)) = \{L \mid L \text{ decided by some DTM in } O(t(n)) \text{ time}\}\]

Example

  • \(\{0^k 1^k \mid k \geq 0\} \in \text{DTIME}(n \log n)\)
  • \(\{0^k 1^k \mid k \geq 0\} \in \text{DTIME}(n)\) (with multi-tape TM)

docs.title: The Class P
docs.text:
Cobham-Edmonds Thesis

Any "reasonable" deterministic model of computation is polynomially equivalent.

Definition of P

\[\mathbf{P} = \bigcup_{k \geq 0} \text{DTIME}(n^k)\]

= Problems solvable in polynomial time

docs.title: Theorem: CFLs ∈ P
docs.text:
Theorem

Every context-free language is in P.

Proof: CYK Algorithm

Step 1: Convert to Chomsky Normal Form

  • Every rule: \(A \to BC\) or \(A \to a\)
  • Parse tree for string of length \(n\) has \(\leq 2n - 1\) nodes

Step 2: Dynamic Programming

Define: \(T[i,j] = \{A \in V \mid A \Rightarrow^* a_i \ldots a_j\}\)

Case Formula Base \(T[i,i] = \{A \mid A \to a_i \in R\}\) Recurrence \(T[i,j] = \bigcup_{k=i}^{j-1} \{A \mid A \to BC, B \in T[i,k], C \in T[k+1,j]\}\)

Complexity:

  • \(O(n^2)\) subproblems
  • Each: \(O(n \cdot |R| \cdot |V|^2)\) work
  • Total: \(O(n^3)\) ✓

docs.title: Non-deterministic Time
docs.text:
Definition

For NTM \(U\), running time \(f(n)\) = max steps over all branches on inputs of length \(n\).

Definition of NP

\[\mathbf{NP} = \bigcup_{k \geq 0} \text{NTIME}(n^k)\]

= Problems decidable by NTM in polynomial time

docs.title: Polynomial Verifiability
docs.text:
Alternative Definition

Language \(L\) is polynomial verifiable if \(\exists\) polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that:

Property Meaning Efficient \(V\) runs in poly-time Complete \(x \in L \implies \exists y: V(x,y) = 1\) with $ Sound \(x \notin L \implies \forall y: V(x,y) = 0\)

docs.title: Theorem: NP = Polynomial Verifiable
docs.text:
Theorem

\(L \in \mathbf{NP} \iff L\) is polynomial verifiable.

Proof

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Given NTM \(U\) for \(L\):

  • Certificate \(y\) = accepting branch choices
  • Verifier simulates \(U\) deterministically along \(y\)

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Given verifier \(V\): 

NTM U = On input x:
  1. Guess certificate y (|y| ≤ poly(|x|))
  2. Run V(x, y)
  3. Accept iff V accepts

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Boolean Formulas

Term Definition Literal \(x_i\) or \(\overline{x_i}\) Clause Disjunction: \(x_1 \vee x_2 \vee \overline{x_3}\) CNF Formula Conjunction of clauses Satisfying Assignment Truth values making formula TRUE

SAT Problem

Input: Boolean formula \(F\) in CNF

Question: Does a satisfying assignment exist?

docs.title: SAT ∈ NP
docs.text:
Proof

NTM approach: 

M = On input F:
  1. Guess assignment T
  2. Verify F is TRUE under T
  3. Accept iff verified

Verifier approach:

Certificate = satisfying assignment

docs.title: Polynomial Reduction
docs.text:
Definition

\(A \leq_p B\) (A reduces to B) if \(\exists\) poly-time computable \(f\) such that: \(\(x \in A \iff f(x) \in B\)\)

Lemma

If \(A \leq_p B\) and \(B \in \mathbf{P}\), then \(A \in \mathbf{P}\).

docs.title: NP-Complete Problems
docs.text:
Definition

\(A\) is NP-complete if:

  1. \(A \in \mathbf{NP}\)
  2. \(\forall B \in \mathbf{NP}: B \leq_p A\)

Cook-Levin Theorem

SAT is NP-complete.

See Cook-Levin Proof

docs.title: Proving NP-Completeness
docs.text:
Method

To prove \(B\) is NP-complete:

  1. Show \(B \in \mathbf{NP}\)
  2. Find known NP-complete \(A\) and show \(A \leq_p B\)

Lemma

If \(A\) is NP-complete and \(A \leq_p B\) with \(B \in \mathbf{NP}\), then \(B\) is NP-complete.

docs.title: 3-SAT
docs.text:
3-SAT

SAT where each clause has exactly 3 literals.

Reduction: SAT \(\leq_p\) 3-SAT

docs.title: CLIQUE
docs.text:
CLIQUE

Input: Graph \(G = (V, E)\), integer \(k\)

Question: Does \(G\) have a clique of size \(k\)?

(Clique = complete subgraph)

Reduction: 3-SAT \(\leq_p\) CLIQUE

See Reduction Details

docs.title: VERTEX COVER
docs.text:
VERTEX COVER

Input: Graph \(G = (V, E)\), integer \(k\)

Question: Does \(G\) have a vertex cover of size \(k\)?

(Vertex cover = set covering all edges)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Complexity Landscape

P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME
Class Definition Example P Poly-time decidable Sorting, CFLs NP Poly-time verifiable SAT, CLIQUE NP-complete Hardest in NP SAT, 3-SAT, VERTEX COVER

The P vs NP Question

Open Problem: Is \(\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{NP}\)?

If yes: All NP problems have efficient algorithms

If no: Some problems are inherently hard to solve (but easy to verify)

低级语言的魅力

汇编语言是最接近机器的编程语言，理解它能帮助我们深入理解计算机的工作原理。
